articles.title: Siri Glitches Ruin Reviewer's Test of Apple's New 'HomeView' Smart Speaker
articles.content: Apple has started selling its new HomeView smart speaker, a 7-inch square-with-rounded-corners screen equipped with a built-in camera. It pairs with your iPhone or iPad to offer personalized content from your email or text messages, using facial recognition to identify each family member. But in a video report, one Wall Street Journal reviewer discovered an issue while testing its smart home feature: WSJ REVIEWER: I've spent the last few years turning my home into a smart home that I can boss around with Siri. A smart lock, a special garage door opener, motorized shades, even a Raspberry Pi in my basement hooked up to my router that lets non-HomeKit devices from Ring and Nest work with Siri. It was all going well, the smart home controller of my dreams even. But then... Reviewer: Open the garage door. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app. Reviewer: Siri, you have the Home app, and you're called the HomeView. Open the garage. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Reviewer: Open the smart wifi garage. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app... WSJ REVIEWER: Apple explained that for security reasons, Siri won't unlock your doors or open the garage through the HomeView using voice commands. You can only tap the screen to unlock them. The concern is that someone could shout a command from outside and gain access to your house. This security concern doesn't make much sense to me. This thing can recognize my face, confirm it's me, and pull up all sorts of information from my phone. But it can't recognize me enough to open my garage? Finally I got Siri itself to explain this top-security measure. Siri: For security reasons, I can't unlock your door or open your garage from this device. Because anyone nearby can speak to a shared speaker. Reviewer: But I'm looking at you! You see my face, and you hear my voice! Siri: I understand. But I don't have a camera to see you. And voice recognition alone isn't secure enough for unlocking your home. Reviewer: You don't have a camera? Siri: That's right. This device doesn't have a camera, so I can't see you. I can only hear your voice, which is why I need you to use your iPhone or Apple Watch to unlock the door. Reviewer: I see, Siri. You're gaslighting me. An Apple spokesperson said they'd send out a software update next month that would let HomeView unlock garage doors and other door locks by voice once it's recognized a user. (And Apple said the update would also fix Siri's hallucination that it didn't already have a built-in camera.) In the end, the speakers sounded good, and the reviewer appreciated how Apple's HomeView didn't have ads on its screeh like the Amazon Echo Show. But the device's built-in Siri voice assistant was "about as reliable as a Magic 8 Ball... And the frustration is so real. Sometimes Siri just doesn't get the voice recognition right... Oftentimes, other devices in the room think I'm talking to their Siri... And sometimes Siris just talk to each." iPhone: Siri is built into your device, so you don't need to download... HomeView: Downloading support for Siri. iPhone: To download the Apple Support app, open the App Store on your device, search for Apple Support, and tap get or the download icon. I've installed support. Reviewer (muttering): I honestly could cry. This might be a first — crying. iphone: I'm software, so I don't have feelings. But it sounds like you're going through a difficult moment. It can really help to talk to someone you trust, like a friend, family member, or a professional who can support you". They complained that sometimes Siri "is just slow, or it gets stuck thinking and thinking and thinking." (It took three minutes to answer their young son's question "What's 10 times 40?") They concluded HomeView's facial recognition feature works well, and so does its smart home functionality (especially when they fix its door-unlocking next month). But its built-in…

articles.title: Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival
articles.content: Vulcan lifted off Sunday for the first time in nine months, carrying 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. The rocket failed about 10 minutes into flight. (United Launch Alliance Photo) A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service. It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported . The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased. ULA said it doesn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it will work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible. The company said it holds itself to the standard of mission success. “Today, we did not meet that standard,” ULA said. Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.” The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role. The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now. The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit. The anomaly came about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn, according to Spaceflight Now. The Centaur is powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris. Spaceflight Now also reported that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t identified the cause. Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing. The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program. Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission . Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation. Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9. In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this…

articles.title: KTC heads to CES 2027 with a 31.5-inch 6K Mini-LED display engineered to break records
articles.content: KTC is preparing a 31.5-inch 6K Mini-LED monitor for CES 2027 The KTC M32P2 6K monitor delivers 6,016 x 3,384 resolution at 60Hz Its Mini-LED backlight features 2,304 local dimming zones KTC is preparing to challenge the expensive end of the high-resolution monitor market with a new display scheduled for CES 2027. The upcoming M32P2 combines a 31.5-inch IPS panel with 6K resolution and Mini-LED backlighting, giving professionals another option. Although pricing remains undisclosed, KTC's history of selling advanced displays at relatively accessible prices makes this announcement particularly interesting. KTC brings 6K resolution and 2,304 dimming zones to CES The KTC M32P2 6K monitor sports a 6K panel delivering 6,016 x 3,384 pixels at 60Hz, offering substantially more workspace than conventional 4K displays. The Mini-LED backlight also incorporates 2,304 individually controlled dimming zones, allowing different screen areas to receive different levels of illumination. KTC specifies peak brightness of 1,000 nits when displaying HDR content, while standard viewing conditions get a maximum rating of 400 nits. The panel has a typical contrast ratio of 1,000:1 and supports approximately 1.07 billion colors through its 8-bit plus FRC implementation. Its advertised color reproduction figures include 98% Adobe RGB coverage, 99% DCI-P3 coverage, and complete 100% sRGB coverage. These specifications could make the display relevant to professional image editing and content production, although independent testing will determine actual color accuracy. The company has also included connectivity options covering two HDMI 2.1 inputs and one DisplayPort 1.4 connection, along with a USB-C port supporting the full display resolution while delivering up to 90W of power to connected devices. Additional connections include three USB 3.0 ports, divided between one upstream and two downstream connections, alongside a headphone output. The adjustable stand provides between -5 and 20 degrees of tilt, alongside 110mm of height adjustment for different working arrangements. Buyers can also use its 100 x 100mm VESA mounting points when installing the display on compatible arms or wall mounts. KTC acknowledged that the high-resolution category remains relatively limited, describing its upcoming exhibition units as unfinished products. “We don’t have many 5K or 6K monitors available at the moment. We have these two units at the show, but they are only samples and not launched yet,” a marketing specialist from KTC told TechRadar Pro. KTC's pricing history could make its 6K monitor interesting The biggest unanswered question surrounding the M32P2 concerns its eventual retail price, particularly considering KTC's established reputation for affordable display hardware. Its H27P3 27-inch 5K monitor has previously sold for approximately $530, considerably less than several competing professional displays. The company has also attracted attention with affordable Mini-LED gaming monitors , including its M27T6S, which has appeared at around $300. Those products provide some indication of KTC's pricing approach when introducing display technologies normally associated with more expensive products. However, neither example establishes what the manufacturer will charge for its upcoming 31.5-inch model.
articles.author: Efosa Udinmwen

articles.title: Your next desktop PC for the price of a Ferrari? HP ZGX Fury packs in 748GB RAM and Nvidia GB300 — but prices start at $132,000
articles.content: HP's latest workstation packs 748GB of memory and Nvidia's GB300 processor The ZGX Fury starts at an eye-watering $132,000 LPDDR5X and HBM3e memory combine to provide 748GB total capacity HP has introduced an expensive workstation that brings computing hardware previously associated with large-scale AI infrastructure into an office-sized machine. The ZGX Fury G1n combines Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra processor with an enormous memory allocation designed for demanding artificial intelligence workloads. Its starting price of $132,000 makes it considerably more expensive than conventional professional computers, even before customers consider optional upgrades HP crams 748GB memory into its expensive workstation The mobile workstation combines two different memory technologies, LPDDR5X and HBM3e, with 496GB allocated to system memory and another 252GB dedicated to graphics processing. The LPDDR5X allocation runs at 6,400 MT/s and connects to a 72-core Arm Neoverse V2 Grace CPU, supporting demanding processing workloads. Meanwhile, the HBM3e memory is integrated into Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra GPU, providing dedicated high-bandwidth capacity for graphics and AI operations. Customers opting for additional graphics hardware can increase the available video memory to 276GB through selected configurations. Together, these components provide the advertised 748GB capacity, although customers purchasing additional graphics hardware can increase available video memory to 276GB. HP also offers configurations featuring discrete Nvidia RTX PRO workstation graphics cards, including the RTX PRO 2000 and RTX PRO 4000. The memory capacity serves a particular purpose beyond running conventional office applications or demanding professional software. Developers and researchers working with large language models can use the machine to process substantial workloads without depending entirely on remote computing infrastructure. HP says the available memory can accommodate local adjustment of language models containing up to 100 billion parameters. The system can also perform inference using models reaching one trillion parameters through FP4 quantization, although actual performance depends on workload requirements. Liquid cooling and networking accompany the $132,000 price Running powerful computing components inside a relatively compact enclosure introduces thermal management requirements that ordinary desktop cooling systems cannot necessarily accommodate. HP therefore equips the workstation with liquid cooling alongside a 1,600W Titanium-certified power supply. The device ships with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, making Linux its supplied operating system rather than Microsoft's Windows environment. This configuration caters to developers and technical professionals who need software environments suitable for demanding computing and AI development. Networking is another important component, with an Nvidia ConnectX-8 SuperNIC providing two QSFP112 connections rated at 400Gbps. These connections allow multiple machines to communicate through high-speed networking when organizations need additional computing resources. The enclosure also supports installation inside a 5U equipment rack, giving organizations another deployment option beyond placing it beneath an office desk. This flexibility allows organizations to deploy the workstation individually or install multiple units inside equipment racks for larger computing operations. Getting all these specifications will cost $132,000 for the standard configuration, enough to buy a brand-new 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQL, although not quite a Ferrari. Customers opting for the RTX PRO 2000 configuration will pay $133,000, while the more powerful RTX PRO 4000 option raises the price to $136,000. At these prices, the ZGX Fury is unlikely to attract ordinary desktop buyers looking for additional memory or improved everyday computing performance. articles.title: GTA 6's Upcoming Launch Celebrated by Wendy's, YouTube, the City of Miami, and 20% of America's Workforce
articles.content: Fast food restaurant Wendy's drew an image of their redheaded mascot in the style of GTA, posting it on social media with the message "Our ride-or-dies are gonna love what we have in the works," and the date 11/19/26. That's how widespread the hype has become for Thursday's release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The BBC reports that fictional brands from the game are now actually appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game's "Vice City" setting. And GamingBible.com reports Rockstar Games has announced Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival, "a real-life music festival to be held in Miami, Florida... on November 21, 2026. Featuring two stages, the festival will be headlined by some incredible artists that, to state the obvious, feature on the game's soundtrack...." YouTube said pre-launch videos about the game have already racked up a whopping 40 billion views (with 900 billion views for videos about all GTA games). And now YouTube is partnering with Rockstar Games to offer several special features on launch day: Fans can drop themselves directly into Vice City using the GTAVI: Visit Vice City Shorts Effect. The feature includes multiple iconic backgrounds, making it easy for creators and fans to build their own launch-week videos... Listeners can find the official GTAVI soundtrack (featuring Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need") and the complete GTA series anthology playlist directly on the YouTube Music homepage throughout launch week... Starting November 19 at 12 AM ET, fans worldwide can tune in to youtube.com/youtube for a 24 hour stream packed with live gameplay, creator podcasts, and original content featuring top creators... [On launch day] fans can jump straight into the global broadcast by clicking the custom GTAVI-themed YouTube logo (Yoodle) on the YouTube homepage At one one study suggests nearly one in a five U.S. workers plan to skip work on Thursday, writes the New York Post: Roughly 18% of workers plan to take Thursday off to park themselves on the couch and wreak havoc across the revamped Vice City, according to data from BambooHR, which analyzed information from 3.4 million US-based employees... Half of the joystick jockeys planning to take off will simply call in sick instead of requesting time off, BambooHR reported. The hordes of workers playing hooky could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity, International Business News reported. Forbes reports the game has $1.18 billion in pre-orders from 12 million buyers, according to market research firm Sensor Tower, puting it ahead of Grand Theft Auto V, which had 7 million pre-orders. The BBC points out that "Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history. This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it. But that's a problem for other games, reports GamingBible.com: With most current-gen consoles having somewhere between 512 GB and 1 TB of free storage before expansion upgrades, it means if you're a gamer with lots of games installed, you're going to have to make some sacrifices and delete any older games you're not currently playing. As reported by Push Square, it seems that Electronic Arts is also getting the message, as it allegedly is showing messages inside games asking players not to uninstall in anticipation of the GTA VI launch. GamingBible.com notes one final concern for hardcore gamers. "Rockstar Games recently confirmed the game targets 30fps, even on high-end consoles like the PlayStation Pro. While it probably won't affect the game's total sales, many gamers are appalled." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The iPhone 18 Pro's C2 modem has transformed my terrible signal
articles.content: It's fair to say that the headline-grabbing arrival of the iPhone Duo has made the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feel a little less shiny than they otherwise might have. Indeed, upon opening my new iPhone 18 Pro Max and restoring my data from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro Max , it was hard not to feel a little disappointed by the lack of bells and whistles on Apple’s latest flagship. That’s probably to be expected from a single-generation upgrade — and, to be fair, I don’t usually swap phones after just one year — but there is one feature that’s caught my eye during my time with my iPhone 18 Pro Max, and it’s been a game-changer for my everyday life: Apple’s new C2 modem. An underrated upgrade I don't believe it: is that strong 5G signal? (Image credit: Future) I’ve been using iPhones for around two decades, but since moving to a more remote area in 2021, I have noticed that my mobile signal has been incredibly inconsistent (on some days, it's absolutely awful). In truth, this spotty signal has been the bane of my digital life, both as a small business owner and a parent — I could be in the same spot on different days of the week and experience completely different levels of coverage. Worse yet, my recent iPhones have had a tendency to display a weak 5G signal when, in fact, there's been no signal at all. With the iPhone 18 Pro Max, however, I’m seeing drastic improvements in signal strength just about everywhere I go. Rather than awkwardly trying to fumble through phone tasks using train or café WiFi, I’ve actually been able to use my paid-for data plan consistently, which has made my iPhone 18 Pro Max feel less like a very expensive iPod and more like a piece of cutting-edge computing. And that’s all thanks to the C2 modem. What is the C2 modem? The C2 modem features in all iPhone 18 Pro models, but not all iPhone 18 Pro Max models (Image credit: Future/Jacob Krol) Apple debuted its C1 chip in the iPhone 16e , and the C2 makes its debut in the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The C2 features in every iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo model sold worldwide, but only in iPhone 18 Pro Max models sold outside of the US. If you’re in the US and have Apple's larger Pro model, you’ve got Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem. Apple hasn't yet disclosed why this is the case, but we suspect it's a result of contractual obligation (we know it's not a technical limitation, since the C2 modem features in all other iPhone 18 Pro Max models, and indeed even in iPhone 18 Pro models sold within the US). As you'd expect from a numbered hardware upgrade, the C2 modem improves on the C1 in several ways. It adds full mmWave support alongside the C1's existing sub-6GHz 5G capabilities, and consumes less energy than its predecessor. There are other iPhone 18 Pro-specific advantages, too: “If an iPhone encounters congested data networks, the phone’s [A20 Pro] processor can signal to the modem which traffic is the most time-sensitive and put it ahead of other data transfers,” Apple told Reuters of its C2 modem. There are dozens of us! Thankfully, I’m not alone in feeling the benefits of Apple’s C2 modem. Plenty of other iPhone 18 Pro users have found that the addition of this small feature is leading to much better 5G connectivity. My C2 Apple Modem Experience So Far: iPhone 18 Pro vs Pro Max from r/cellmapper Of course, as this Reddit post mentions, a new modem will only help if you’re in an area covered by 5G in the first place. Luckily for me, my home isn't so remote as to rely on older-generation networks, but that's worth bearing in mind if you live out in the sticks (Apple's hardware wizardry can only work so much magic). And don't get me wrong: a new 5G modem is hardly the most exciting upgrade on a phone that costs at least $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099, and perhaps it's the least we should expect from Apple when the year-on-year upgrades are so limited elsewhere. Still, after years of awkwardly lifting my iPhone into the sky…

articles.title: Nvidia engineer leaves company over lack of transparency around Jensen Huang’s exit, details decision
articles.content: Just days after Jensen Huang suddenly resigned from his position at Nvidia , an Nvidia Robot Research Engineer said that he would leave the company as well. But more than just showing support for the former CEO with a generic “I stand with Jensen” message, Darrel Dai laid out several reasons for the decision on X . I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.That is why this has been so disappointing.I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close.I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me.These are my personal views. November 15, 2026 “What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me,” the engineer posted. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.” It seems that Jensen Huang has gained the respect of the people working under him, with many calling for his reinstatement despite the many controversies he is currently facing. There’s also an online petition demanding that the Nvidia board “Bring Jensen Back,” with over 150,000 signatures at the time of writing. Nvidia is centered around Jensen Huang, with the former chief executive reportedly having a small army of 60 people directly reporting to him. But despite his busy schedule and legendary persona, Dai said that “Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly,” and that “It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.” Dai also pointed out that “employees’ trust and sense of belonging” are part of what makes a company great. articles.title: Apple's Smart Glasses Strategy Hinges on Siri and iPhone Apps
articles.content: Apple plans to unveil its first smart glasses at WWDC in June 2027 and begin shipping them before the end of the year, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman . In the latest edition of his "Power On" newsletter , Gurman shared new details about the glasses' design, charging system, and Siri features. Current prototypes of the glasses, internally code-named "N50," are reportedly slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans. Some test units have oval camera openings integrated into the frame without protruding housings. A front light indicates use or charging, while Apple is experimenting with additional privacy features. Apple is apparently developing multiple styles and colors, with an emphasis on materials, sensors, and audio quality. Employees have described the sound as "industry-leading," with the glasses supporting music playback, calls, and FaceTime audio. Testers can also charge the prototype glasses while wearing them. A flat, three-pin magnetic connector, "roughly the size of a Tic Tac," attaches near the end of the left temple arm. Gurman said it remains unclear whether Apple will use this charging system in the shipping product. The first model will not display augmented reality imagery. Wearers will interact through ‌Siri‌, which will use the cameras to answer questions about their surroundings. Planned uses include identifying buildings, suggesting meals based on ingredients in a refrigerator, providing directions, and translating signs and conversations. Apple also intends to support calls, messages, iPhone notifications, calendars, standard and visual reminders, music controls, and smart home controls. To support the glasses, developers will need to let ‌Siri‌ control specific features in their iPhone apps. Apple envisions tasks such as booking restaurant tables, requesting rides, ordering coffee, shopping, and purchasing movie tickets working on the device. Developers will not need to create separate apps for the glasses. Their software will run on a paired iPhone, with the two devices working together to fulfill requests. Current plans require a recent iPhone model, with no Android support. The paired phone will compensate for the glasses' limited processing power and memory. Wi-Fi will allow certain functions outside third-party apps to remain available without a nearby iPhone. Gurman suggested audio playback could theoretically continue over Wi-Fi, although the glasses will not function as a fully independent device. Internal prototypes purportedly run a reduced version of visionOS 28 and contain a processor derived from older Apple Watch chips. Other custom components handle wireless connectivity and process images as the cameras capture them. Apple began introducing the necessary ‌Siri‌ controls in this month's first iOS 27.3 beta, enabling more precise control of app actions. Originally demonstrated in 2024, the capability has been rebuilt using newer AI models. Apple plans to release support for its own apps in December, followed by third-party support in 2027. Apple wants developers to prepare those integrations before the glasses arrive and continues to target a WWDC announcement next year. The company sees access to its existing app ecosystem as a major selling point against rival smart glasses. The device will also overlap with camera-equipped AirPods, which remain scheduled for launch in late 2027 and will also provide ‌Siri‌ with information about the user's surroundings. The glasses should offer longer battery life and accommodate more sensors, with Apple seeing the potential for them to be worn throughout the day. Work on the glasses started in the early 2020s, and Apple is said to have largely settled on the hardware. The remaining obstacles involve software and AI, which Gurman said are running late and could delay the planned 2027 launch. articles.title: Huawei Set To Challenge Tesla Powerwall with New, 20 kW Home Battery
articles.content: "Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery," reports Electrek: This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla's latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark... The Chinese tech firm is calling it an "all-in-one residential energy system" that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that's available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW. The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei's proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It's so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes. Huawei's basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with "just" 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That's enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you'll want to keep going if you're preparing for more than a day or two without power. If that sounds like you, Luterra's got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can keep scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel. Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Cockpit-Simulator 737X CDU (v2) Review: An Essential Component for Flight Sim Enthusiasts
articles.content: Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits. Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment. Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024. The Real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality. The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot. (Image credit: flaps2approach.com) The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys. Build Quality Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell. The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator. The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck. The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch. The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup. The Feel (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button. Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) For our testing inside of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, we used the PMDG 737-800. We flew the following routes: 45 minutes from Las Vegas, Nevada to Ontario, California 2 hours from Phoenix, Arizona…

articles.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 stock returns to Newegg with 21 models
articles.content: After rumors of Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards being withdrawn from the consumer retail channel, it is pleasing to see major U.S. e-tailers like Newegg stuffed with stock today. Checking out this popular online electronics retailer, we note that there are 21 RTX 5090 SKUs available , and 11 are sold by and shipped by Newegg. Sadly, pricing remains in 3x MSRP+ territory at the time of writing. Remember, you can sift through pricing trends in our comprehensive GPU price tracking 2026 feature to see that Nvidia's Blackwell flagship was once available at its fabled sub-$2,000 price. (Image credit: Newegg ) Despite what looks on the surface like an ample supply (but there are order limits of one per customer), prices for RTX 5090s remain extremely high. The best prices we can see at Newegg are $6,599, but this price applies only to a water-cooled Aorus model and another sold inside a Gigabyte AI BOX eGPU . They might still appeal to you, depending on your setup, though. For a ‘standard’ air-cooled graphics card, albeit a very nice Aorus RTX 5090 Master , you’ll need to squeeze at least $6,659 out of your savings. A bonus with this card, alongside several others from the Gigabyte stables now purchasable from Newegg, is that it comes with a free motherboard. Many of these Gigabyte Aorus designs are being bundled with a full-ATX-sized X870 Aorus Elite WIFI7 AM5 motherboard , purportedly worth $319. Please note that the same motherboard is available to purchase outside this bundle for a more reasonable $249. If you have money to burn, there are plenty of even more expensive SKUs to pick from. There are no opulent Golden Dhabab models on Newegg, sadly, but you’ll still be asked to part with $11,896 for the Asus ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 Edition 20 (sold by a Newegg marketplace partner). Perhaps surprisingly, given recent trending pricing news, that’s the only model above $10K, but there are still many models that are almost $10,000 from Asus, MSI, and Zotac. Even an Nvidia Founders Edition RTX 5090 refurb is priced at $8,899. In context, these RTX 5090s are still at astronomical prices for consumer gaming PC add-in hardware. But they are now purchasable from a big retailer with fast delivery, rather than off a random scalper. It was only a month ago that rumors swirled about the RTX 5090 and the RTX 5080 being withdrawn from retail. That seemed to trigger crazy levels of price inflation, and reports of $10,000+ prices for the flagship card seemed to become the norm. One can only hope that stock continues to flow to Newegg and other outlets, and RTX 5090 / RTX 5080 prices will settle lower as a result.

articles.content: Apple’s smart glasses are reportedly ‘slightly thinner’ than Meta’s 2nd gen Ray-Ban glasses above. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge Apple's smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. articles.title: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica
articles.content: Environmental activist Bill Gates has "quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America's No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services," reports ProPublica, in a new 5,000-word investigation. But inspectors from America's Environmental Protection Agency "have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place." While Gates has invested at least $2 billion in green companies, he's "put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry," their article argues. And Gates has increased his stake in Republic "to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion." While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They're responsible for as much as a fifth of the country's emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.... [Gates] has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor... "It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic's behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits," said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder... Gates didn't respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn't find any public comments he's made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic's shares — "It's 'Garbage In' for Gates," the New York Post headline read — the company's stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows... A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune [in 1999]... To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he'd given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets... After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates' stake in Republic over the years that followed. [On behalf of the Gates Foundation] Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic's main competitor, Waste Management. Methane emissions weren't a major focus of climate activism until years later The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it's responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack
articles.content: The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer. The moniker came from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ), who have announced a fight against this crime wave, starting with the seizure of associated cloud infrastructure. According to the DoJ , North Korea is behind these attacks, stealing cryptocurrency to fund its government. The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the important details. The agency's techs seized "cloud-based infrastructure," containing 900 videos of targeted victims. FaceStealer is an advanced form of spear-phishing, complete with AI deepfakes, usage of the victims' contact networks and personal information, and carefully orchestrated preparation — sometimes months in advance. The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts. The largest heist attributed to FaceStealer is the recent Binance hack that saw thieves make out the proverbial door with over $5 billion (most of it thankfully frozen and/or recovered), but far from the only one. The FBI attributes about $400m in stolen cryptocurrency to the campaign, and importantly, also notes that the hackers have repeatedly tried to sneak into open-source software, chiefly Javascript/NPM modules and Rust crates. Despite not being mentioned by name, one example hack is almost certainly the Axios compromise from March 2026. The Node/Javascript library sees about 100 million downloads a week, and temporarily contained a remote-access tool — thankfully for only a few hours. Jason Sayayman, the Axios developer in question, got hooked by an attacker posing as a legitimate company interested in hiring him. The malfeasants replicated the CEO's persona, created a Slack workspace with legitimate-looking channels, then invited him to a Teams meeting with multiple "people." This modus operandi is what the FBI warns about . According to the bureau, FaceStealers start by getting access to a person's communication application(s), then lifting all previous conversations, contact lists, and, most importantly, stealthily recording video of them and/or their contacts. The footage and information will then be used to catch the actual targeted victim, who'll often be sent offers for jobs or investment opportunities. The victim will eventually be invited to a Zoom or Teams meeting that's actually hosted on an attacker-controlled server, with a typo-squatted domain like "uu01webzoom.us" or "teams.livemeet.us". The meeting will often have deepfaked AI participants and/or previous meeting recordings playing, granting the event an air of legitimacy — particularly because conversations leading up to this point will contain real information and context. At some point, though, there will be some sort of "technical problem," and the victim will be prompted to install an "update" or software to fix the problem, which is loaded with malware. From there, the attackers have free rein over the victim's computer and data, and will siphon off browser sessions, CI/CD passwords, and all manners of access credentials to eventually get access to cryptocurrency wallets — or just use this information to find a juicier target, like the poor Binance developer through which Binance's hot wallets were broken into. The FBI says that the above scenario may play out in multiple cycles until the attackers reach their intended target, collecting loads of precious video and information along the way to make the final strike much more convincing.

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy
articles.content: Many AI startups are moving fast without a clear direction. (GeekWire Illustration / ChatGPT) The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy. “Hope is not a strategy, and neither is speed.” A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line. Five arguments for speed, and what’s wrong with four of them Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing. Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed. The window is closing . Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one. Competitors are everywhere . AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.” The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box. The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data. Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction. Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed. Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into. Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures. Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not. “Some decisions are consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible – one-way doors – and these decisions must be made methodically, carefully, slowly, with great deliberation and consultation.” — Jeff Bezos, 2015 letter to shareholders Judgment and defensibility: what…

articles.title: Face ID & telephoto lens are coming to iPhone Duo, eventually
articles.content: While the timetable isn't clear, Apple is reportedly working on adding Face ID to the iPhone Duo . However, the effective engineering deadline for the late 2027 refresh is coming soon, and the feature may not make the cut. Face ID is coming to iPhone Duo, but when is anybody's guess Apple reportedly has two main priorities for the second-generation iPhone Duo. Those are, sensibly, adding Face ID , and adding an Action Button. We've spoken about the Action Button before, and the most likely implementation is a combination with the camera control button. But, the loudest complaints we've heard about the model is about the lack of Face ID. A report on Sunday morning by Mark Gurman claims that prototypes exist with Face ID, with integration into having the VCSEL for the biometrics on the outer display. articles.title: 357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery
articles.content: A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors. At sheets. works/data-viz/cpu-dies, you will find a sortable, searchable, and filterable gallery featuring the outstanding, freely shared die shots from the likes of Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz . Find one or two of your favorites, and peer into the details to enjoy a nostalgic technological trip down memory lane. That’s what I did. (Image credit: sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies ) The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way. Beneath a brief introduction that credits the skilled photographers who share these images for free, you can glide through the 357-photo collection. By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first. Those browsing the gallery can instantly switch to a True Scale gallery view, too, which provides some physical sizing context. The next view option for the gallery is a table, where you can see processor maker, year, die dimensions , and photo license at a glance, but it sacrifices visual impact by showing just tiny thumbnails. sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies Navigating the gallery is also quick and intuitive thanks to a built-in search function. Using this, it was easy to display only 486 CPU s, for example. For your information, there are 17 486 CPU variants in this gallery with samples produced by AMD, Cyrix , IBM, TI, UMC, VLSI, and Intel of course. You can click any of the thumbnails to jump to a larger view with notes of the design, as well as photographer details/credits. Though that click zooms in the image considerably, I found that a right-click – open image in new tab - was needed to enjoy the die shot’s full visual splendor. It would be great to see the database/gallery maintained with the latest shareable die shots from the various contributors. Also, it could be improved by fully populating details such as the die area, which is not always present. Some more searchable and sortable fields, such as transistor count, might also make this resource more satisfying. For my personal nostalgia, I enjoyed seeing CPUs like the Motorola 68000 and the AMD Athlon XP up close. Surprisingly, some eras, including the Intel Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, seemed underrepresented, though.
articles.author: Mark Tyson
articles.fingerprint: 1971 2024 357 cpu crammed detailed die gallery into shots spanning

articles.title: The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it
articles.content: The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well. However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box. more…

articles.content: Apple could finally announce its smart glasses during WWDC 2027 with privacy-focused features built around the Secure Exclave and Siri AI . articles.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
articles.content: Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck . German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024 , which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the issue wasn’t caught earlier. This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still. Aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few big tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: Rust Leaves Top 10 in TIOBE Index, Making Room for Go
articles.content: "In November's edition of the TIOBE Index, Rust has dropped out of Top 10," writes I-Programmer, noting that Rust ceded the #10 position to Go. "At the same time, another Google-originated language, Dart, has entered the top 20 ousting Julia after only one month." TIOBE explains Dart's popularity is mainly being driven by Flutter, Google's framework for building cross-platform mobile applications. In fact, Flutter has become one of the major technologies for cross-platform mobile app development. The Dart language itself is not particularly unique, although it incorporates many modern programming language features. Its success is largely driven by the strength of the Flutter ecosystem and the convenience of developing applications for multiple platforms using a single codebase... [In November's ranking] Visual Basic has also lost two places, making room for R and SQL in the Top 10. Further down the ranking, Assembly has re-entered the Top 20. So TIOBE ranks the top 10 languages in November as Python, C, Java, C++, C#, JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, and Go. But I-Programmer points out that "At the top of the table, Java is back in the top 3, after over three years in 4th position," pushing C++ down to #4. Are some changes more significant than others? If you think of the ratings as shares of a pie divided into 100 pieces, there is one huge slice — Python, accounting for a over a fifth of the pie, then comes C with a slice slightly less than half of Python's. Java and C++ then have smaller slices... and C#'s share is around half of their average size. Over half the pie has now been shared between just five languages... — Next 5 (#6-10): 10.17% (JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, Go) — Next 10 (#11-20): 11.12% (Rust, PHP, Fortran, Scratch, Perl, MATLAB, Assembly, Swift, Delphi, Dart) — Next 30 (#21-50): 12.81% — Final 50 (#51-100): 12.93% [So in this month's chart...] Java has overtaken C++, but as you can see from this month's Top 10 chart they are in lock step and the difference between them is insignificant. More obvious is that Python is way ahead of all the competition and that C has an edge over Java and C++. For more discussion of this see TIOBE — Two To Rule Them All in which Mike James argued that this: confirms the standard model of programming - code is written in Python and C and everything else is just noise. Back in July we reported Rust Enters TIOBE Top 10. After four months in #10 Rust is now back at #11, which is still three places above its position, 14, a year ago. Given the way these rankings operate it only takes a very small month-on-month change for a language to lose its position and even, as has happened here it can gain in terms of its percentage ranking while still moving down. So Rust with 1.63% in November is now in #11 when it had been in #10 with 1.44%. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge
articles.content: Judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix , has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed. According to the decision , the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some new evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the big three memory chip manufacturers. Go deeper with TH Premium: Memory (Image credit: SK Hynix) AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers The future of DRAM: From DDR5 to future ICs High-bandwidth memory roadmap Inside the history of DRAM price-fixing lawsuits Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is. Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that. “Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.” The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year. One of the events they cited included the “simultaneous DRAM production cuts” from October 2022 to April 2023, which was quickly followed by a “coordinated pivot to HBM.” They also said that the three companies announced the winding down of DDR4 production in a span of three months and have failed to expand the production capacity “despite these extraordinary prices — the single most powerful supply signal the DRAM industry has ever produced.” Other factors that the suing parties brought to the table include the introduction of stringent customer vetting procedures in response to the shortage, the refusal to sign long-term contracts for DRAM customers, Micron’s decision to shut down Crucial (its consumer memory brand), multiple statements projecting the shortage , as well as their involvement in previous price-fixing scandals. The big three memory chip makers argued that all of these are logical business moves so that they can maximize their revenue during a period of great demand and that they are “consistent with [their own] independent self-interest.” They also said that they appear to have similar behaviors because they’re in a highly concentrated market, and that they’re all “reacting to the same market pressures,” thus it would make sense for them to have a similar response. Despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward. This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision. Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.

articles.title: DuckDB has an answer to “bloated” database messages
articles.content: Older database protocols were built before big data. Some still send results row by row, repeating details like column names and types with every row. The result, says DuckLabs product team lead Guillermo Sánchez Dionis , is “quite a bloated message.” That overhead adds up when you’re moving large query results. DuckDB’s answer is Quack , an HTTP-based protocol that streams query results in batches of column data as DuckDB produces them. It was previewed in May and was released in October as part of DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS. On this latest episode of The New Stack podcast, recorded at DuckLabs headquarters in Amsterdam, Sánchez Dionis explains how that design lets developers start working with results while a query is still running. A database protocol is a formal set of rules and message formats that dictates how a client application communicates with a database server. It acts as a specialized language that lets a software application securely send SQL queries, receive structured data tables, and manage transactions over a network. It handles connection and authentication, query packaging, data serialization, and error management. But according to Sánchez Dionis, most protocols were designed pre-big data for other types of systems, with serialized rows rather than columns. They also add a lot of unnecessary data, he says, like column types and column names per row. “It becomes quite a bloated message. That already makes the protocol not only not good for analytical systems, but it’s also quite heavy,” he contends. As protocols evolved for analytical systems, they did start using columns, but “they were still doing things like serializing one value at a time and other things that are really not efficient. Modern systems are trying to converge on using vectorized execution to be able to serialize more values at a time and trying to use more efficient representations of columnar data formats to send over the wire.” All while the Quack protocol, he says, is aiming for a different, highly efficient approach. Quack is DuckDB’s HTTP-based client/server protocol, with its first production release shipping in DuckDB 2.0.0 on Oct. 21. Not only does this signal Quack moving out of the preview stage, but the protocol now offers certain developer-friendly features: The CONNECT statement allows developers to attach to and query a remote Quack server via standard SQL commands. The new -serve CLI argument instantly starts a Quack server instance from the command line, and -connect connects to one. Multiple clients can write to the same database concurrently, with transactions handled under DuckDB’s multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) isolation. “Quack uses DuckDB’s data chunks — which is our columnar representation of data. We also serialize in a very efficient manner because we are a vectorized engine. We also make sure that we send the results in a streaming fashion,” Sánchez Dionis explains. “One of the most important things is tightly coupling the engine. Once you start producing results, instead of waiting for the query execution to end and then serializing all of the results at once, you serialize and send results as they are emitted by the engine. Therefore, the client can keep consuming results without having to stop the engine.” For developers, he says, that means they don’t have to do anything. “I think the biggest advantage that you will see is you will have a very small memory footprint” “You run a query from the comfort of your laptop, and you just get streaming results back. I think the biggest advantage that you will see is you will have a very small memory footprint,” he says. “What’s cool about Quack is that you install and load it wherever you are. You can also create another client on the [same] laptop with the Quack extension, and they will communicate…
articles.author: Jennifer Riggins

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5: Same scores at almost 4x the cost
articles.content: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9 and said it beats Claude Opus 5.5 in almost every capability the company measured. In the same announcement, it recommended starting with Opus for most coding and knowledge tasks, calling it its “strongest daily driver.” I wanted to find out why a company would steer people away from its best model, and whether the cheaper one really is enough. …why a company would steer people away from its best model, and whether the cheaper one really is enough. On Anthropic’s coding benchmarks , Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% at Xhigh effort on FrontierCode 2.0, compared with 45.5% for Opus 5.5 at Max. Anthropic also reports that Fable scored 45.3% at High effort at roughly half the cost per task of that Opus run. On FrontierSWE v2, the company reports 69.9% for Fable and 62.3% for Opus. Fable’s standard API rates are twice Opus’s: $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, versus $4 and $20. Twice the price should make a meaningful difference, so I gave both models three coding and agent jobs and measured how well they did, how many tokens they used, what they cost, and how long they took. My tests are much smaller than Anthropic’s benchmarks and can’t prove or disprove those scores. The tests I ran each model once per test through Anthropic’s API at default settings, with no turn cap. Anthropic’s API defaults on Fable and Opus aren’t equal. Fable 5.2 runs at high effort, and Opus 5.5 runs at medium, so these results show what a developer gets without tuning anything. I used a script to grade each answer the model gave for each test. The dollar figures are estimated API costs based on reported token usage. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately. Here are the tests I ran: Cron scheduler : I gave each model a written spec for code that runs when the next scheduled job runs, then sent a change request. I used a hidden suite of 50 tests to grade the final code. Invoicing repo fix : Each model worked as an agent in a small invoicing library with interacting bugs in rounding, discounts, tax, and shipping. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit. Incident investigation : Each model used a terminal to find the cause of a payments outage from logs, metrics, and deployment records. The data included decoy deploys and servers with wrong clocks. The models tied with perfect scores on the first version of every test, so I made each test harder and reran it twice. Cron scheduler This test checks whether a model can turn a detailed spec into correct code and then absorb a change without breaking it. Here’s what differed between the versions. Version 1 : The spec covered standard cron schedules, such as every 15 minutes or weekdays at 9 a.m. Version 2 : I added rules like “the weekday nearest the 15th” and “the last Friday of the month,” and the change request reversed how two fields combine. Version 3 : The code had to handle time zones and daylight saving time by hand, without Python’s time zone library. Both models scored 50/50 on all three versions. The difference was in how much work each one did to get there. Fable 5.2 wrote two to three times as much reasoning as Opus 5.5 on every version. The extra reasoning did not raise Fable’s score on any of the three versions. The extra reasoning did not raise Fable’s score on any of the three versions. Across the three scheduler versions, Opus matched Fable’s scores in 358 seconds versus 661 and cost an estimated $0.99 versus $3.29. The numbers: Version 1 Fable 5.2 : 2 turns, 14,471 in, 18,732 out (11,122 reasoning), $0.87, 170 s. Opus 5.5 : 2 turns, 8,055 in, 9,431 out (3,846 reasoning), $0.22, 80 s. Version 2 Fable 5.2 : 2 turns, 20,215 in, 23,990 out (14,627 reasoning), $1.12, 226 s. Opus 5.5 : 2 turns, 14,090 in, 15,991 out (6,695 reasoning), $0.38, 131 s. Version 3 Fable 5.2 : 2 turns, 21,121 in, 28,254 out (17,452 reasoning), $1.30, 265 s. Opus 5.5 :…

articles.title: The Silicon-Carbon Battery Breakthrough Behind 7,000mAh Smartphones
articles.content: For almost five years, phone batteries were stuck. Flagships from Apple, Samsung, and Google hovered around 4,500 to 5,000mAh, and "two-day battery life" was something only chunky gaming phones could promise. Then, in about 18 months, everything changed. The OnePlus 15 ships with 7,300mAh. Tecno has put 8,000mAh into a phone that is 7.42mm thick . Honor sells a phone with a 10,000mAh battery that is 8.3mm thick . None of this came from making phones bigger. It came from changing one material inside the battery. Here is what silicon-carbon batteries are, why they work, what they cost you, and why the iPhone and Galaxy in your pocket probably still don't have one. What changed inside the battery Every lithium-ion battery has two electrodes. When you charge your phone, lithium ions move from the cathode into the anode and are stored there. When you use your phone, they move back, and that flow powers the device. For decades, the anode has been made of graphite. Graphite is cheap, stable, and predictable, but it has a hard limit: it can hold one lithium ion for every six carbon atoms . Once the industry had squeezed out almost all the efficiency it could from graphite, the only way to add capacity was to make the battery physically bigger. Silicon changes the maths. Per gram, silicon can in theory store 4 to 10 times as much lithium as graphite, according to LG Energy Solution. Even a small amount of silicon in the anode raises how much energy fits in the same space. That is what a "silicon-carbon" battery is: a normal lithium-ion battery whose anode mixes silicon into a carbon structure instead of using graphite alone. The cathode, the electrolyte, and the way you charge it stay basically the same. Why not just use pure silicon? Because silicon swells. When it absorbs lithium, it can expand to several times its original volume: by up to 300% when fully charged , according to Android Authority. A phone battery that grew like that would crack its own electrodes within a few charges, and it would push against the screen and the back of the phone. Manufacturers manage this in three main ways: Small amounts of silicon. LG Energy Solution says its first silicon anode for EV batteries, in 2019, used about 5% silicon. OnePlus says the "Silicon NanoStack" battery in the OnePlus 15 uses up to 15%. The rest is still carbon. Nano-sized particles. Very small silicon particles crack less when they expand than large ones. A carbon "cage". The silicon is embedded in a carbon matrix that gives it room to swell and spreads out the mechanical stress. The result is a battery that is denser than graphite but still behaves well enough to survive years of daily charging. How much difference does it make? Estimates vary: Android Authority puts the gain at roughly 10 to 20% more capacity in the same space, while How-To Geek cites 20 to 50% . In practice, that is roughly the difference between a 5,500mAh battery and a 7,000mAh battery without making the phone any thicker. Phone makers have spent that extra capacity in two ways: Bigger batteries in normal-size phones. This is the OnePlus 15 approach: a regular flagship body with a much larger battery inside. Thinner phones with normal batteries. Foldables benefit the most. A book-style foldable is two thin phones joined by a hinge, so every millimetre matters. Some brands have pushed the first approach to the extreme. Honor's 10,000mAh phone and Tecno's 7.42mm, 8,000mAh phone would have been impossible with graphite anodes a few years ago. The trade-offs nobody puts on the box Silicon-carbon batteries are a real improvement, but they are not free. They may wear faster. Even with all the engineering above, silicon still expands and contracts on every charge. Over hundreds of cycles, that stress adds up. A battery engineer interviewed on the Waveform podcast said these batteries tend to lose more capacity in their first two to three years than conventional cells, according to 9to5Google.
