articles.title: Survival Under the Allowlist: A Sharded, Agent-Assisted Design for Censorship-Resistant Networks
articles.content: How internet control moved from blocklists to allowlists, why today's circumvention tools struggle with that shift, and a design sketch that combines local AI agents, sharded relay discovery, and a thin web3 coordination layer. 1. Introduction: When the Internet Becomes a Privilege For a long time, the mental model of internet censorship was a blocklist. An authority decided that certain domains, IP addresses, or keywords were forbidden, and the network enforced it. Everything else worked. Circumvention was a race: find a path the list did not cover. That model is eroding. In 2025 and 2026, several things happened at once: In Russia, mobile internet shutdowns became routine, and during them only a short list of approved services stayed reachable. Global Voices reported that on 27 September 2025, shutdowns were recorded in 54 regions and whitelists of available sites were active in 30 of them. In Iran, a nationwide shutdown began on 8 January 2026, and a second one followed from 28 February. Monitors described the second as the longest nationwide blackout on record, with fewer than one percent of users able to connect at one point. When access was partially restored in late May, Iran International reported that it came after nearly three months of blackout and remained heavily filtered. In China, a leak of internal documents from a Great Firewall vendor showed that the same technology had been deployed outside China , in countries including Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar, and Kazakhstan. This article does two things. First, it gives a unified technical picture of how modern network control works, drawing on published measurement research and reporting, so that readers who are not specialists in this field can see the whole system. Second, it proposes a design direction, built from existing research, that tries to answer a specific question: what would a circumvention network look like if it assumed that allowlists, per-ISP differences, and AI-assisted blocking are the normal case? A note on scope. Iran, China, Russia, and North Korea are used here as points on a spectrum rather than as targets of an indictment. Iran is a particularly instructive hybrid, because its infrastructure draws on both Chinese and Russian technology (more on that below). The focus is technical: how the systems work, where current tools fail, and what might do better. Nothing in this article is a finished invention. Most building blocks come from published research. The contribution, if there is one, is the composition, and an honest list of what remains unsolved. This design also sits in the decentralized-AI stack. The agent runs small models on the user’s device (edge inference) rather than calling a central inference API, route intelligence is shared through a ledger with no single operator, and the aim is an AI-assisted network that is hard for any single party to switch off. 2. Four Eras of Network Control The shift can be summarized in four overlapping eras. This is a simplification, since all four coexist in different places, but it is a useful frame. Era Model Typical techniques Example evidence 1. Blocklist Everything works except listed targets DNS poisoning, IP blocking, HTTP blockpages OONI's 2014–2017 Iran measurements found DNS injection and transparent proxies serving blockpages, with circumvention-tool sites themselves blocked and Tor blocked on many networks 2. DPI and traffic classification Inspect traffic and block what looks suspicious Protocol fingerprinting, SNI inspection, active probing The Great Firewall's passive detection of fully encrypted traffic (first reported in November 2021); SNI-based QUIC blocking from April 2024; Russia's TSPU boxes 3. Allowlist Nothing works except listed targets Blocked-by-default networks, approved-user tiers, whitelisted IP ranges Russian mobile whitelists (2025); Iran's tiered access during the 2026 shutdowns 4. Isolation A domestic network is the default; the global internet is exceptional…

articles.title: Why Skydio Built a Lopsided Drone
articles.content: Skydio’s drones have always been magical. From MIT research and early prototypes to what I would argue is still the most advanced consumer drone ever made , this is a company that makes very cool stuff. Sadly, Skydio no longer makes cool stuff for consumers , instead focusing on drone platforms for public safety, inspection, and other things that, on a good day, don’t affect me personally. Even so, a new drone from Skydio is worth paying attention to, especially when it’s as weird as this one—the F10 Lightrunner is a fixed-wing camera drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight, all while looking so lopsided that it’s surprising that it can actually fly. The benefits of asymmetrical aircraft There’s a short rabbit hole you can go down if you start looking for other examples of asymmetrical aircraft. In the 1990s, legendary aircraft designer Burt Rutan and his company Scaled Composites built some decidedly odd airplanes, including the Model 202 Boomerang . But perhaps the most famous asymmetrical aircraft was the Blohm & Voss BV 141 , a World War 2-era reconnaissance plane that featured an engine in the middle alongside a crew compartment alarmingly offset out onto the right wing. The unique design was intended to give the crew the best possible view for reconnaissance missions, because in a typical single-engine aircraft, the crew sits right behind the engine, limiting forward visibility. Nearly 90 years later, the Skydio F10 is applying a similar philosophy to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, which typically track targets by flying around them in circles. “While turning at low altitudes, it becomes very hard to avoid occluding a camera with a wing or a tail,” explains Andrew Goessling , director of engineering at Skydio. “So we were analyzing a lot of these use cases, and one of our engineers just blurted out, ‘what if we put the camera on the wingtip?’ And that’s where it all started, because as long as you only turn left, a lot of these problems just go away.” Of course, putting the camera on the F10’s wingtip creates a bunch of new problems, chief among them that the aircraft is no longer balanced. Not only is the camera payload fairly heavy relative to the total mass of the drone, but its bulk also creates greater drag. This is why the seemingly straightforward solution of putting something else (like a battery) on the other wingtip to rebalance the drone isn’t practical, says Goessling. “The issue there is that the camera represents a substantial portion of the total aircraft drag, so putting something else on the other wing would cut your flight time nearly in half.” The F10’s wing-mounted camera payload necessitated asymmetrical wings and uneven motor placement. Skydio Goessling points out that there’s nothing inherently bad about an asymmetric design like the F10; it just makes the life of engineers either a little more difficult or a little more exciting, depending on your perspective. “There were really two challenges here: What is the optimal design for an aircraft with a wingtip camera, and then once you have the design, how are you going to control it?” Any fixed-wing aircraft design has to consider three factors: distribution of mass, how thrust is distributed between the motors, and how the shape and location of the wings affect the aircraft’s aerodynamics. Once Skydio decided on their requirements for the F10—including the wingtip camera, two motors to enable controllable hovering for takeoff and landing, and a high top speed and long flight time—the engineers used a modeling and optimization approach to explore design options. The resulting aircraft compensates for the wing-mounted camera payload by extending just that wing to provide more lift on that side, and repositioning the motors asymmetrically to balance thrust against the added drag of the camera. articles.title: LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
articles.content: LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy . If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off) , respectively. LG B6E OLED TV Where to Buy: $1399.99 $699.99 at Best Buy (55-inch) $1899.99 $999.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $2699.99 $1499.99 at Best Buy (77-inch) Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6 , the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform. The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

articles.title: How We Reached 99% Line Coverage in a React Native App
articles.content: In October, the mobile app's CI report showed 99.26% line coverage. The number was gratifying, but it was a poor place to start the story. When I joined the consumer engineering team in April, the app had 113 unit-test files and 14 Maestro YAML files. The device flows had existed for years, yet they were not running in CI. A feature could be finished while the work of trusting it still sat ahead of us. My remit as engineering manager covered mobile, backend and web work. Mobile verification was a particular bottleneck because a change could bring a nearby screen back into scope. People repeated checks near release, often without leaving an executable record for the next change. I wanted the checks to arrive with the implementation, where a developer and reviewer could see what had been exercised. There is no April coverage percentage in our records. I can't turn 113 test files into an imaginary baseline. The six-month comparison is about the test inventory and the way those tests entered development. The October coverage report is a later measurement of a defined scope. Tests became part of finishing a change In May, we began making tests an expectation for changed production code. The agent working on a task had to understand the requirement, implement it, write relevant tests and run the repository checks before presenting the result. The tests were written close to the change, while the intended behaviour was still fresh. We gave that work some practical support. Jest ran with jest-expo and a shared render helper that supplied providers and routing. Business decisions that did not need a screen could live in pure helpers. Controlled GraphQL responses made it possible to exercise failure states without bringing up the whole application. These choices made a useful test cheaper to write and easier to keep. The count moved gradually at first: 164 unit-test files at the end of May, 250 in June and 395 in July. It rose to 1,040 in August and 1,669 in September. At the October checkpoint, the inventory contained 2,257 files. That is a substantial record of work. A file can contain one assertion or many, though, and splitting a file changes the count without protecting another behaviour. The device checks had to run too The Maestro inventory followed a different path. It stayed at 14 YAML files through April, reached 129 in May and 225 by the end of September. October's snapshot had 404. Those files include leaf flows, shared setup and suite entrypoints, so they do not represent 404 independent journeys. The more important step was connecting device flows to execution. The first EAS device workflow arrived in May; PR smoke runs and nightly Maestro Cloud runs followed in June. A flow sitting in a folder could now return a result during development. Even then, an inventory count was generous. The October route report found that all 99 non-exempt product routes were reachable through leaf flows in the repository, while only 28 were reached by leaves that CI ran. The gap was visible, which meant we could plan the next work instead of calling the whole app covered. What October's 99% measured The October line-coverage report merged results from four Jest shards. It counted 22,903 covered lines out of 23,072 eligible lines within the configured scope. The reported figure was 99.26%. The report also recorded 95.55% branch coverage, a useful reminder to look at decisions and failure paths as well as lines reached. We had made the coverage scope more explicit. Test helpers, Storybook, development-only code and other excluded files no longer belonged in the production-code denominator. That made the result more useful for the decision it was meant to support. It also means a coverage percentage without its scope is easy to overread. We pinned CI thresholds to the measured October baseline so a later change could not quietly lower that measure. Coverage still cannot tell a reviewer whether an assertion would catch the bug that prompted a…

articles.title: Five Reasons Businesses Lose Money on Payments
articles.content: Businesses closely monitor their finances, customer acquisition costs, and conversion rates. However, businesses can still lose money after a customer clicks the Pay button. Dmitry Sinegubov, Chief Commercial Officer at FinteqHub , explains how this happens and what businesses can do about it. Ishan Pandey: A business records thousands of successful payments. Why doesn't this necessarily mean that all the money has been received? Dmitry Sinegubov: There is a record in the company's internal system, a record maintained by the payment provider, and the actual settlement. These records do not always match. For example, an online store may mark an order as paid, while the payment provider reports that the transaction was declined. Or a refund may have already been processed, while the internal system still records the funds as received. Transaction amounts may also differ, and certain fees may go unaccounted for. However, not every discrepancy represents a financial loss. Some may result from delays in updating transaction reports. When a company works with multiple payment providers using different reporting formats, manual reconciliation quickly becomes a significant operational challenge. Our Reconciliation Tool automatically compares transaction records from the client's platform with those from payment providers, identifies discrepancies, and lets financial specialists focus only on cases that require investigation. Ishan Pandey: Shouldn't finance departments simply hire more employees as payment volumes increase? Dmitry Sinegubov: Transaction volumes grow faster than employees can process and reconcile them manually. Suppose a company connects five new payment providers across different countries. Each provider has its own reporting formats, transaction statuses, settlement schedules, and refund procedures. Finance specialists must download reports, consolidate spreadsheets, identify duplicate transactions, and investigate discrepancies. Hiring additional employees may temporarily solve the problem, but as transaction volumes grow, so do operational expenses and the risk of human error. Effective automation does not necessarily mean removing people from the process. Instead, it means eliminating the need for employees to manually verify transactions that already match. The system automatically handles standard cases and refers only disputed or exceptional transactions to human specialists. Ishan Pandey: How can a technical failure turn into a financial loss? Dmitry Sinegubov: Imagine a customer attempting to pay for an order, but the payment gateway stops responding. To the customer, this looks like a typical payment error. For the business, however, the situation is more complicated: the transaction may have failed, been processed successfully, or the payment confirmation may simply have failed to arrive. Automatically retrying the transaction without checking its status could result in a duplicate charge. On the other hand, doing nothing may cause the customer to abandon the purchase entirely. This is why payment infrastructure needs more than just backup processing routes. It also requires accurate transaction status management, properly controlled retries, and mechanisms for handling uncertain transaction outcomes. FinteqHub's AutoRouting system includes primary and fallback processing routes, along with safeguards for situations where standard routing rules cannot be applied. However, a fallback route is not a universal solution. In some cases, retrying a payment is unsafe until the outcome of the original attempt is known. articles.title: How Will AI Affect Open Source Development?
articles.content: This week the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) announced it would broaden its AI security resources, including a new guide to finding and fixing vulnerabilities using AI, "from preparing and sandboxing AI to validating, fixing, and preventing issues." The guide "stresses that AI-generated patches should never be trusted without automated tests and human review. An online course (LFD126) is planned for the coming months." OpenSSF also released the State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026 report (supported by OpenSSF, ActiveState and the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation). And it turns out the 2026 report "found a growing gap between the pace of AI-driven software development and organizations' ability to secure the code being produced." 58% of surveyed teams ship code faster than security reviews can keep up, while 60% say AI coding assistants have increased the number of external packages in their codebases. This data underscores the importance of trusted, reliable guidance as AI deployment continues to grow. Meanwhile the Linux Foundation announced at this week's Web Summit that it was releasing a new study on "how commercial open source companies generate revenue, convert users into customers and build their businesses," emphasizing the question's new relevance in the age of AI. "AI now writes code almost for free, and that raises a hard question for the whole software industry: if code costs next to nothing, where does the value of software lie?" Commercial open source [COSS] companies have been answering that question for more than 30 years. They have built large businesses on code they give away, which makes them a good guide to how software will make money in the age of AI... Seventy-two percent of respondents report a net positive impact from AI, against 8% negative. So far, the gains show up mostly inside companies. Internal productivity is the most cited benefit (73%), ahead of market expansion (46%) and new monetization opportunities (39%). AI roles are the only hiring category growing on net. COSS strategy is mostly unchanged by AI. But when companies do adapt, they are nearly twice as likely to open more of their core product rather than become more closed. When asked what sets them apart, 57% of companies name brand recognition and trust, well ahead of enterprise features, integrations and community size. They turn that trust into revenue through support and services (63%), managed cloud (49%) and open core (43%). Most combine these: 65% run two or more revenue models. Companies stack models as they grow, rather than switching between them: managed cloud rises from 35% of companies below $5 million ARR to 66% above $20 million. Venture-backed companies lean toward open core (53% vs. 38% for others). The report draws on a survey of 225 commercial open source founders and enterprise leaders (published by Linux Foundation Research in partnership with Serena, and with sponsorship from AWS, Red Hat, Futurewei and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. And when it comes to open source, "over half of founders point to brand recognition and community trust as their greatest asset," said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. So "The findings from this year's report prove that AI isn't a threat to commercial open source software — it's an accelerating tailwind. With 72% of companies viewing AI as a net positive primarily driving internal productivity, the ecosystem is leaning further into collaboration." The Linux Foundation's announcement includes an interesting perspective from Matthieu Lavergne, partner at the venture capital company Serena. "Open source won the developer. Next, it will win the agent. The 225 founders we surveyed mostly see AI as a productivity gain today, but that's only the start: agents are set to become open source's largest users, and they choose what is open, proven and trusted. The founders who build and price…

articles.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
articles.content: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people's lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities. Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people's impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences. A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity. Read full article Comments

articles.title: The best apps that are actually built for foldables
articles.content: Credit: Brady Snyder / Android Authority Last month at the Android Dev Summit, we learned Google plans to start taking foldable apps much more seriously . While there’s a growing number of foldable apps out there, Google wants to bring extra attention to the highest-quality options by offering boosted visibility and more prominent placement. The specific terms or criteria for the plan have yet to be fully divulged; this seems like a positive sign for foldable users looking for apps that can take advantage of the extra real estate. While the program might not be ready, the good news is that there are already quite a few solid foldable apps out there. Let’s take a look at just five of the best options that we recommend.

articles.title: Google's 20-Year-Old Chubby Design Still Has Useful Lessons for AI Infrastructure
articles.content: Distributed systems rarely fail because engineers don't understand consensus. They fail because every application ends up implementing its own version of coordination, ownership, and failure recovery. In 2006, Mike Burrows presented a different approach in The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems at OSDI ( pdf ). Rather than exposing consensus as a programming primitive, Google built a centralized coordination service with a familiar file-system-like interface. Applications could use it for distributed locking, naming, and storing small amounts of critical metadata without implementing the underlying coordination logic themselves. Chubby was deliberately designed for coarse-grained, advisory locking and low-volume, highly reliable storage. It prioritized reliability and simplicity over raw throughput. Its deeper contribution was an architectural decision: make coordination a shared infrastructure responsibility rather than an application-specific problem. Nearly two decades later, that decision remains relevant. Modern AI infrastructure faces many of the same coordination challenges, although the workloads and failure modes have changed. Distributed ingestion pipelines, vector databases, inference gateways, and GPU workers all need reliable mechanisms for managing ownership and shared state. This article revisits the original Chubby paper and examines what its design principles can teach us about building reliable LLM infrastructure. The Core Argument: The Design Boundary Before Chubby, distributed applications often implemented coordination mechanisms independently or relied on specialized infrastructure services with limited generality. Although Paxos provided a foundation for distributed agreement, turning consensus into a practical application-facing service required additional engineering around leader election, failure detection, client retries, naming, and lock semantics. Chubby changed where that complexity lived. Instead of asking every application to implement distributed coordination, Google provided a reusable service that handled the difficult parts behind a relatively simple interface. The design choices documented in the paper reveal an important separation of responsibilities. Advisory, not mandatory locking. Chubby locks are advisory. The service grants and maintains lock ownership, but it does not automatically prevent an application from accessing an external resource without holding a lock. Participating clients must respect the locking protocol. This keeps Chubby decoupled from application semantics, but it places responsibility for correctness on the clients and the resources they access. Leases and coordinator stability. Chubby uses time-bounded leases to manage coordinator authority and support reliable failover. A replacement coordinator must respect the previous coordinator's lease before taking over. However, lease expiration alone is not sufficient to protect external resources from stale clients. Chubby also uses sequencers to help clients and protected services distinguish operations associated with valid lock ownership from those issued by an earlier lock holder. Coarse-grained locking. Chubby deliberately avoids fine-grained locking. Applications typically lock entire files or directories rather than individual records. This reduces coordination overhead and makes the service easier to reason about. The trade-off is that applications must design their locking strategy carefully to avoid unnecessary contention. Low-volume, high-reliability storage. Chubby provides reliable storage for small amounts of critical metadata. It was never intended to replace a general-purpose database. Its purpose was to make configuration, naming information, and other coordination-related state reliably accessible. The important architectural decision is the boundary between the coordination service and the application. Chubby manages ownership, synchronization, and shared metadata.…

articles.title: Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
articles.content: Australia's central bank sees early signs that AI is hitting young entry-level workers in highly exposed jobs like software development and customer service. Since ChatGPT launched, job postings and employment among 15- to 24-year-olds in those fields have dropped more sharply than among older workers. Author Mike Major cautions against jumping to conclusions, however, noting that business cycle shifts and remote work trends could also explain the numbers. The article Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.title: Bland Launches Tofu-1, a Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech Model for Calls
articles.content: Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, has released Tofu-1 , a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview. The Tofu-1 speech-to-speech model targets calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out, with no transcript between. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . What is Tofu-1? Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models. How does Tofu-1 differ from a cascade voice agent? Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech. Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly , so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture. Audio understanding Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page: Speaker tracking: tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing. Noise separation: separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones. Paralinguistics: hears hesitation, frustration and urgency. Full duplex and thinking while talking Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early. Scene generation Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise. What is Bland’s ‘TV Test’? The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output. How does Tofu-1 compare with other full-duplex models? FDB results use different benchmark versions and are not directly comparable. How can teams access Tofu-1? Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises. Bland names banking, healthcare, insurance and government as target sectors. The sign-up form asks for monthly call volume, from under 1,000 to 50,000+. Key Takeaways Tofu-1 is Bland’s first full-duplex speech-to-speech model, built for noisy calls. It hears audio directly: speakers, background noise and caller emotion. The only number is self-reported: over 92% could not spot it in screenings. No size, latency, pricing or benchmarks yet; rivals publish latency and tool-use scores. articles.title: Bluetooth HDT could finally fix wireless audio quality, but there’s still one big problem
articles.content: News that Bluetooth has officially adopted its new High Data Throughput (HDT) specification should be music to audiophile ears far and wide. And there’s a good chance your future pair of wireless headphones could sound considerably better as a result. If you missed the announcement, Bluetooth HDT extends the capabilities of Bluetooth Low Energy (LE), boosting its maximum physical-layer data rate (PHY, pronounced “fie”) from 2Mbps to a comparatively colossal 7.5Mbps. That’s almost four times the maximum rate of conventional Bluetooth LE, and 2.5 times faster than Bluetooth Enhanced Data Rate (EDR), which tops out at 3Mbps.

articles.title: AI is making software easier to build. Keeping it running is another story
articles.content: These days, it almost feels like old news: Developers can now use AI tools to generate code , build features, and make changes in a fraction of the time they once needed. The problem now surfacing across businesses is that once software goes into production, teams still need to monitor, maintain, and fix it. A feature that takes minutes to build can introduce problems that take engineers hours to investigate. Google’s 2025 DORA report , based on responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals, found that greater AI adoption was associated with faster software delivery but reduced stability. While the researchers didn’t establish that AI-generated code directly caused more outages, their findings suggest that companies can produce software faster without necessarily becoming better at maintaining it. That raises a critical question for companies investing heavily in AI coding tools: If development keeps getting faster, how much of the work involved in running software can also be automated? A growing group of companies is working to find out, developing AI systems that can investigate failures, identify possible causes, and, in some cases, take corrective action without waiting for an engineer. MORE SOFTWARE, MORE TO MANAGE Ishay Yaari, cofounder and CEO of DataAgent , a company developing autonomous remediation software, says the operational side of software development hasn’t advanced at the same pace as coding. “More code, more frequent deployments, and more infrastructure changes naturally create more potential failure points,” he tells Fast Company . For site reliability engineering (SRE) teams, that means managing applications and infrastructure that may be changing more frequently. When something fails, engineers must figure out what changed, identify the cause, and restore service. Consider an application that begins crashing after an update. The cause could be faulty code, an incorrect configuration, insufficient computing resources, or a problem with another service. While monitoring tools may detect the failure immediately, engineers still need to examine logs, review recent changes, and investigate several possibilities before deciding what to fix. Yaari says companies often respond to growing complexity by adding monitoring tools and collecting more data. That can help engineers see what’s happening, but it can also mean more alerts to investigate without necessarily improving how quickly problems are resolved. The pressure isn’t necessarily coming from poor-quality AI-generated code. Even reliable code can be difficult to manage when applications, infrastructure, and dependencies are changing frequently. In a recent analysis of AI-assisted development, Google’s DORA researchers found that developers saved time generating code but spent more time reviewing and verifying it. They also emphasized the importance of testing, feedback, and established engineering practices in turning faster development into better results. For companies, that means the benefits of AI coding tools may depend partly on what happens after developers finish writing the code, particularly the ability of SRE teams to keep applications running reliably. GIVING AI THE KEYS TO PRODUCTION Software monitoring and observability tools have traditionally helped engineers detect problems and understand their causes. Now companies are trying to automate more of the response. DataAgent is pursuing that approach. Its platform is designed to monitor applications and cloud infrastructure, identify potential issues, and help investigate them. Yaari wants AI to take on more of the operational work engineers currently perform manually. Some failures have familiar remedies. An application might repeatedly crash because it doesn’t have enough memory. A deployment might fail because of an incorrect configuration. Or a new release might introduce errors that disappear when the system returns to an earlier version. Companies already use automation to address…

articles.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
articles.content: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

articles.title: The chip war never ended
articles.content: It’s no secret that the world runs on computer chips. This became clear during the pandemic, when a race for even basic chips needed to operate cars and other devices set back manufacturing timelines across the world. Beltway policymakers are reminded of just how important semiconductors are to the world every time China seems to move toward invading Taiwan, which raises the specter that the country could subsume control of TSCM, the most prominent computer chip contract manufacturer. Now Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia , which comes after reports of at least three known extramarital affairs—one of them with an alleged spy for the Chinese government—has thrown the world’s supply of computer chips back in the spotlight. With stocks falling and no obvious succession plan, it’s not clear what the future of Nvidia is right now, or how it might jostle the broader semiconductor ecosystem. “Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors,” says Chris Miller, a Tufts University professor and author of the 2022 book Chip War , which documents how the world came to depend on these tiny components. Fast Company chatted with Miller on November 12 about Washington, D.C.’s response to the Huang scandal, Nvidia’s future, and the prospect of keeping advanced semiconductors out of countries like China. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. You’ve followed the chip industry for quite a long time. Are you surprised by what’s happened over the last few weeks? Jensen was an extraordinary CEO for 33 years, since Nvidia’s founding. [He] deserves a lot of the credit for the company’s extraordinary rise, but also deserves a lot of the blame for a series of poor decisions that have led not just to his ouster, but to a period of crisis for the company. Jensen really was central to Nvidia’s success, and he ran the company in a pretty unique way. He had 60 different people reporting to him directly, so there wasn’t a sort of standard corporate hierarchy, which worked really well for a long time. But it means that now that he’s gone, it’s not obvious who can fill his shoes. There’s not really a deputy who was waiting in the wings to take over. I’m curious about the history of espionage attempts like what’s being alleged here. There is some history during the Cold War, for example. There were efforts by spies from the Soviet Union or Eastern European countries to get access to sensitive technology by getting close to semiconductor executives. But I think the scale of this is kind of unique. First, that it happened to such a central company in the U.S. tech ecosystem, the most valuable company in the world. That’s somewhat unique. The second thing that’s unique is that the affair in question was both with a major customer, which shouldn’t have happened, as well as an [alleged] Chinese intelligence asset. There were a series of failures of judgment for a person who was one of the most important people in the U.S. and really in the entire world’s technology sector, and that combination does make this case unique. I’m wondering about unexpected winners or companies that stand to benefit from this happening, especially other companies in the GPU market. There are going to be competitors of Nvidia that will see this as an opportunity to win market share. AMD, for example, produces GPUs like Nvidia. In addition, many of Nvidia’s key customers, firms like Amazon—which has a vast data center business—buy Nvidia GPUs, but also design their own chips that have comparable performance characteristics. Many companies that have in the past relied on Nvidia will be watching very carefully to see whether they can rely on Nvidia going forward, and if not, they might turn to competitors. articles.title: I recently tested the flagship Dreame X50 Ultra Complete robot vacuum and was impressed by its cleaning capabilities — and it's $200 off in this early Black Friday deal
articles.content: As a Reviews Writer here at Tom's Guide, I spend most of my time testing out the latest robot vacuums . Now, they say never to work with children or animals, but that's where the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete thrives — it makes sure all the mess they leave in their wake is taken care of. Since recommending this robot vacuum to a friend with children and pets in her home, it's great to see a $200 price drop on the flagship robot vacuum in this early Black Friday deal . You can now purchase the Dreame X50 Ultra Complete for $1,099 on Amazon . It's an impressive gadget that's pretty much self-sufficient and can even climb over small inclines with retractable legs. It excels on hard floors and can mop up any mess with its circular mop pads. The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete excels on hard floors with its side-sweeping arms, mapping navigation, low-maintenance base station, user-friendly app, and stylish design. View Deal My favorite thing about this robot vacuum is the extended reach. Most standard vacuums try their best to get ot the edges of the room, but almost always miss the corners. The Dreame X50 Ultra Complete is a little different because its side-sweeping arms and mop pads can get into all the gaps the robot can't quite get to. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Speaking of getting into small spaces, the sensor on top of the vacuum is retractable. This means that it can easily get under low furniture up to 3.54 inches high. During testing, it easily made its way under my low-lying sofa, and the LED lighting came on to guide the way. (Image credit: Tom's Guide / Millie Fender) The retractable legs are the real star of the show here. They help the robot make its way over small ledges, high-pile carpets, and even obstacles like table legs. It's a very helpful assistant to have in the house and makes cleanup after a busy day much easier. You can find out more about the robot vacuum by reading my full Dreame X50 Ultra Complete review .

articles.title: Stop doing sit-ups — a yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach recommends this exercise to work the core, hip flexors, and back muscles
articles.content: Did you know that when it comes to building core strength and stability, sit-ups and crunches aren’t the best place to start? Unless you perform them with perfect form, sit-ups and crunches can stress your lower back and neck because you repeatedly bend your spine forward under load. What’s more, if, like me, you’re a runner or spend a lot of time sitting behind a desk, there’s a high chance your hip flexors take over during this move. This can pull on your lower back, causing discomfort. Instead, yoga instructor and strength and conditioning coach Melissa Leach recommends a simple yoga pose to build deep core strength and spinal stability. Read on to find out more. As a reminder, if you’re a complete beginner, pregnant or postpartum, or returning to fitness following an injury or surgery, this might not be the right move for you and your body. It’s always best to seek personalized advice from a qualified professional. How to do boat pose The move Leach recommends over sit-ups and crunches is the boat pose. "Boat pose is one of the most efficient core exercises because it doesn't just isolate the abs; it engages the hip flexors, glutes, pelvic muscles, and back all at once, helping build functional core strength rather than working one single muscle in isolation,” she says. All you’ll need is your bodyweight, but using one of the best yoga mats can help make things more comfortable. “There are different ways to perform boat pose. Traditional holds usually consist of staying in the pose for a total of 25 breaths, broken into five sets, while others add movement by hinging the upper body upward and downward,” says Leach. “This version is a more accessible entry point for beginners, starting with bent knees and shorter, more manageable holds.” (Image credit: Future) Sit on the floor with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor Lean your torso back slightly while keeping your spine long and your chest lifted Engage your core and slowly lift your feet off the floor, bringing your shins parallel to the ground Balance on your sit bones, avoiding rolling onto your tailbone Once stable, extend your arms in front of you, with your palms facing each other at shoulder height If you feel comfortable, you can slowly extend your legs to create a ‘V’ shape with your body Hold for 20-30 seconds, and repeat 2-4 times “For beginners, keeping your legs bent in a half boat pose instead of straight can help reduce the core strain and effort required at the start. Lightly gripping the backs of your thighs can also provide support to help you balance,” says Leach. “If you struggle with balance and maintaining a straight spine, you can either sit on a folded blanket or cushion to help tilt the pelvis forward, or sit with your back a few inches from the wall for reassurance. “The most important thing is to get a hold of the technique first, so start slowly, only holding for as long as it's comfortable and slowly increasing the length as your core strength improves.” What are the benefits? On paper, this move looks simple, but after 20 seconds, you’ll know it’s anything but. Holding your torso and legs lifted activates your rectus abdominis (six-pack muscles), obliques, and deeper transverse abdominis at the same time. You’ll also work the muscles along your spine, counteracting bad posture from prolonged sitting. (Image credit: Shutterstock) As you hold your legs off the floor, you’ll work your hip flexors, quadriceps, and inner thighs, as well as working your balance and coordination. "Boat pose also helps build stability rather than just endurance. Holding the position forces your deep core muscles, the ones that support your spine and pelvis, to switch on and stay engaged throughout. Over time, this can translate into better posture, a stronger lower back, and a core that supports your everyday movement," Leach adds. articles.title: Hate dragging out the ladder? Clear your gutters from the ground with these 3 vacuum attachments instead
articles.content: Few home maintenance chores feel more daunting than clearing clogged gutters. Dragging an extension ladder across uneven flowerbeds, leaning precariously over shrubs, and scooping wet sludge by hand is both exhausting and genuinely dangerous. Ignoring the buildup is not an option either, as overflowing gutters quickly send rainwater pouring down your siding and pooling against your foundation. The trick to clearing your roofline safely comes down to extending your reach from the ground, removing loose debris before you add water, and knowing when a clog is too stubborn for a pole attachment. Why you shouldn't put off cleaning clogged gutters As damp leaves and pine needles pack together, they form a heavy dam that blocks rainwater from reaching the downspouts. That trapped water spills over the lip of the trough, soaking fascia boards until the wood rots and saturating the soil around your foundation walls, where leaks and basement dampness soon follow. In colder months, standing water inside a blocked gutter also freezes solid, adding enough weight to pull brackets loose from the roofline or form damaging ice dams under your shingles. Here are three simple ways to clear your gutters cleanly while keeping both feet firmly on the ground. The easy way to clear gutters from the ground 1. Pull dry debris out with a wet/dry vac gutter kit Blasting leaves out with a leaf blower works over open grass, yet it creates a mess over decks, patio furniture, or flowerbeds. A gutter attachment kit for a standard wet/dry shop vac keeps that debris contained while letting you work safely from the lawn. (Image credit: Craftsman ) Brands like Craftsman sell these universal kits at hardware stores and Amazon. Each kit includes three or four rigid plastic extension wands that click together into a 10-to-14-foot pole, topped with a curved, U-shaped nozzle. Hold the assembled pole like a pool skimmer, hook the curved nozzle over the gutter lip, and switch the vacuum on to pull dry leaves, twigs, and grit straight down into the canister beside you. Work in short sections along the wall, lifting the hook over each gutter bracket as you walk , and wear eye protection and gloves in case stray debris drops from above. Gutter Cleaning Attachment Kit: $27 This four-piece accessory kit fits Craftsman and most other wet/dry vacs with a 2-1/2-inch hose, giving you two rigid extension wands, a curved gutter nozzle for suction, and a blower nozzle to clear dry leaves safely from the ground. View Deal 2. Lift stubborn clumps with a telescopic gutter scoop If your debris is too damp for a vacuum to lift, grabbing a hose right away will only turn the leaves into heavy, wet paste. (Image credit: Shutterstock) Instead, attach a curved gutter scoop or stiff brush to a telescopic extension pole suited to your roofline height. Work in short sections and focus on lifting material up and out of the channel rather than pushing it toward the downspout , which only packs debris tighter into the outlet. If you cannot see over the lip of the trough, clipping a small pole-mounted inspection camera to the shaft lets you spot any leftover buildup without guessing. 3. Flush the channel gently with a curved hose wand Once you have removed the bulk of the leaves, you still need to clear fine shingle grit and confirm that water can actually escape down the pipe. (Image credit: Shutterstock) Hook a curved garden-hose attachment over the gutter lip and run a gentle stream of water rather than a high-pressure blast , which can loosen gutter brackets or force water up under your shingles. Work toward the downspout to wash remaining dirt away. If water starts backing up over the edge, turn the hose off immediately rather than adding more water, as a persistent blockage inside the downspout elbow usually needs to be cleared by hand. articles.title: 3 acclaimed sci-fi movies on HBO Max with 90% or higher on Rotten Tomatoes — including a Stanley Kubrick classic that changed the medium
articles.content: As First World problems go, losing your evening to non-committal HBO Max scrolling isn't ideal. It's way too easy to just stick on your 14th "The Sopranos" rewatch on the HBO streaming service, rather than give a potential sci-fi classic you've never seen before a much-deserved (and overdue) viewing. That's where my obsessive cinephile colleagues and I are here for. We all watch movies with great passion. For me, it's what gets me out of bed in the morning. Though I don't always personally agree with Rotten Tomatoes ratings — how is "The Matrix" only at 83%?! — the trio of HBO Max pictures I've picked out for you are all excellent, and all scored at least 90% or higher. Anyway, the following three sci-fi flicks are all streaming now on HBO Max, and each one is stellar. So get them watched ASAP. ‘2001: A Space Odyssey’ (1968) It's utterly appalling that I only saw “2001: A Space Odyssey” for the first time post-COVID. Stanley Kubrick’s seminal sci-fi opus is a mind-bending watch in the best possible way. It looks incredible, the final act is both spellbinding and slightly mystifying, and it easily boasts one of the most iconic scores of all time. It’s a five-star masterpiece. Yet I shamefully knew of it first for cheeky references in 1994’s “Deep Space Homer” episode from our beloved Springfieldian family, then again during 2023’s “Barbie”, which features a lovely, genuinely funny callback to the iconic monolith scene. And I’d never seen the film at that point! Shameful! Just know that this is the defining Kubrick masterpiece. HAL! Those apes getting comfy up against the monolith! The all-time iconic final scene with the space baby! I know I said it before, but “seminal” really is the only word to describe “2001: A Space Odyssey”. It’s arguably the most important and influential sci-fi movie ever made. RT is doing Kubrick's opus dirty at ‘just’ a 91% rating. Rotten Tomatoes score: 91% Watch “2001: A Space Odyssey ” on HBO Max now 'Dune: Part Two' (2024) I’m fond of “Dune: Part Two”, just as I was of its 2021 predecessor — two movies that pretty much erased David Lynch’s polarizing 1984 version from memory banks. And Lynch rarely dealt in duds. Though I don’t consider him at the level of legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins (an occasional Denis Villeneuve collaborator), Greig Fraser still shoots the mid-part of this epic sci-fi trilogy gorgeously. Do I think “Dune: Part Two” is as good a picture as either Villeneuve’s 2016 “Arrival" (91% RT rating) or my beloved "Blade Runner 2049" (88% RT)? Hell no. But it’s a classy sci-fi sequel that has me all in on this December’s Dunesday. I can’t lie, though. I do think "Part Two" misses the wonderful presence of Duncan Idaho (Jason Momoa). But hey, we still get those colossal sandworms. And new Big Bad Feyd-Rautha Harkonnen (played with a delicious serpent-like venom by Austin Butler) proves a great foil for Paul Atredides. As for our moody duke, Timothée Chalamet continues to nail down his leading man status in films with real smarts. Rotten Tomatoes score: 92% Watch "Dune: Part Two" on HBO Max now ‘Dawn of the Planet of the Apes’ (2014) Can you quickly indulge me in a quick Rotten Tomatoes rant? The fact that “Dawn of the Planet of the Apes” is sitting on the same 91% rating as my favourite ever movie “Jurassic Park”... well, that’s frankly unhinged. The sequel to 2011’s successful franchise reboot “Rise of the Planet of the Apes”, “Dawn” is another well-meaning sci-fi with a heart, strong performances and excellent effects. It just ain’t Spielberg’s dino masterpiece. Rant over. With our simian hero Caesar (another impeccable mo-cap performance from Andy Serkis) now very much in charge of his clan of developed apes, the film’s central conflict occurs when a team of humans tries to repair a hydroelectric dam in monkey territory. Although initial exchanges go badly, the kindly-natured super chimp eventually lets Malcolm (a very good Jason Clarke) fix the dam, and a cross-species…

articles.title: Waking up at night is the biggest barrier to a good night's sleep for over 1,700 Tom's Guide readers — an insomnia expert explains how to stop it
articles.content: We all know how incredible it feels to wake up after a great night's sleep: refreshed, clear-headed and ready to tackle the day ahead. But for many people, nighttime wake-ups are impacting their ability to achieve that. In fact, in a Tom's Guide sleep poll, more than 1,700 of our readers said that waking up during the night it is their biggest barrier to getting good night's rest. The poll showed that this problem far outweighed any of the other common challenges to good sleep, including snoring , not being able to fall asleep sleep and overheating at night. So, to help address this widespread issue, we've spoken to Dr. Saema Tahir , a sleep and pulmonary specialist, to find out more about the affects of nighttime wake-ups, what steps you can take to curb them and how to fall back to sleep if you do find yourself wide awake in the middle of the night. What did the Tom’s Guide survey uncover about the impact of nighttime wake-ups on sleep? (Image credit: Future) Here at Tom's Guide we're running an ongoing sleep poll to find out what is stopping our readers from sleeping well. (Scroll below for your chance to have your say). For almost three months, the poll has asked 'What is your biggest barrier to getting a good night's sleep?' The results so far paint a clear picture of the major issue readers are facing when it comes to sleep: nighttime wake-ups. The overwhelming majority of respondents, currently 69% (more than 1,700 people) of those who have taken part in the poll, selected 'waking up during the night' as their response. ' Can't fall asleep ' comes in second at 17% of respondents, while 'overheating at night' affects 6% of respondents and 'snoring (you or your partner' and 'can't get comfortable' have each currently received 4% of votes in the poll. "There are a variety of different reasons that people wake up throughout the night. So I'm actually not surprised by the data," says Dr. Tahir, a quadruple board-certified sleep specialist, adding that it is "the number one complaint I see in the office as well." The sleep expert explains that that the reasons for nighttime wake-ups range "from behavioural, environmental, medical symptoms of undiagnosed disorders, and there's sleep disorders in themselves that can wake you up in the middle of the night." When is waking up at night a problem? (Image credit: Future) Clearly the results of our poll show that nighttime awakenings are impacting sleep quality for many people — so when exactly does waking at night become problem? A brief wake-up during the night isn't actually abnormal, research shows that it's actually part of how our sleep cycles work. During the course of the night, people typically go through as many as five sleep cycles — consisting of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep that typically last around 90-100 minutes each — and in between each cycle you may briefly awaken. What becomes problematic is something is waking you up or you are unable to go back to sleep. Dr. Saema Tahir "Wake ups, 3 to 4 times, sometimes 5 times a night, are normal. Most people do wake up. They just don't remember them. Or they're able to go right back to sleep. So that is a normal sleep process," says Dr. Tahir, who treats sleep issues including insomnia, circadian rhythm disorders and sleep apnea from her practice in New York. "What becomes problematic is something is waking you up or you are unable to go back to sleep. That's when we think of it as a potential problem, but most people don't realise that we all wake up." How does waking up at night impact your sleep? If you're waking up and not getting back to sleep, Dr. Tahir points out that firstly, you will not be clocking up enough sleep. "And if you're not getting enough hours, you're probably not getting the appropriate architecture. So, you are missing out on, probably, the deeper stages of sleep," she explains. articles.title: I tried this 7-minute micro-workout before every shower for 30 days — is it worth the hype?
articles.content: If you haven't heard of "micromovement" routines, it's like exercise snacking , where you break up sedentary time with mini workouts or chunks of movement, like walks, bodyweight routines, or even a quick jog. According to research from Yoga-Go , you may add eight years to your biological age if you spend a lot of time sitting, which can be eight hours a day or more, regardless of whether you still exercise daily. Determined to start my day on the right foot, I decided to add a seven-minute bodyweight workout to my mornings, and this is what I did and didn't notice after 30 days. Why does micromovement matter? A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness (@tomsguidefitness) A photo posted by The decision to stand rather than sit or to take the stairs over the escalator determines how much movement you fit into your day and how much energy you burn outside of workouts, also known as Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis, or NEAT. Just because you fit a 45-minute HIIT workout into your day doesn't undo the impact of accumulated sitting time, so how often you get up and move about really does matter for your long-term health. 7-minute micro-workout The movements below can help maintain functional strength, relieve stress, combat sedentary time, and move your muscles and joints, which increases oxygen-rich blood flow around the body. Here's the routine I followed every morning for 30 days. Future Future Future Future Shutterstock Shutterstock Squats: Squats build lower-body strength and help you maintain independence as you age. Strong legs and glutes contribute to activities like walking or running, and keep the hips, knees and ankles strong and mobile. Push-ups: Push-ups build strength in your triceps, shoulders and pecs while improving pushing power. Focus on maximal range of motion by extending your elbows, then lowering your chest as close to the floor as you can. Engage your core, and exhale as you press up. Cat-cow: Cat-cows improve spinal mobility and posture awareness and reduce stiffness. Try to increase your range of motion with every rep, inhaling as you drop your stomach and exhaling as you round through your spine. Shoulder blade squeezes: Squeezes strengthen the upper back and improve posture. This is also a great way to increase activity in the rear stabilizing muscles of the shoulders, which supports shoulder mechanics. Keep your shoulders relaxed. Lunges: Lunges are a unilateral strengthening exercise targeting the hips, glutes, hamstrings, quads and calves, improving balance and stability. Reversing your lunge puts less pressure on the knees; forward lunging improves quad emphasis. Sit-ups: Sit-ups strengthen the core, namely the rectus abdominis, which is a large superficial layer of muscles along the abdomen that works as you flex your torso. Focus on keeping your feet pressed into the ground and try to sit upright so that your hands can pass your toes. Supermans: This back exercise works the muscles along your posterior chain, including the upper, mid and lower back, glutes, hamstrings, plus your arms and shoulders. It's a great one to try if you don't have weights to row or pull. What happened when I tried it everyday for 30 days? (Image credit: Future) I love functional compound bodyweight exercises because they target the main muscle groups in your body and they can still feel challenging. If you're short on time and just want to get some movement in while you can, 60 seconds of each move performed back-to-back gives you a seven-minute full-body workout before you've even brushed your teeth in the morning. I love that I could work my chest, shoulders, arms, back, glutes, core and legs without picking up a single weight or worrying over getting to the gym. I hadn't fatigued myself enough that I couldn't then go to Pilates, the yoga studio, or out for a run later in the day, and I had woken up my muscles, oiled my joints and got fresh blood flow pumping around my body while lifting my heart rate. All before I had…

Leading the charge alongside him are top tournament points scorer Jamayne Isaako and equal-top try scorer Casey McLean. articles.title: I’m a professional video editor who just spent two weeks using the MacBook Pro OLED — and it’s such a huge upgrade from my older M1 Max that I can’t go back
articles.content: I preordered my 14-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro in October 2021, the week Apple announced it. It was my first Mac, and I documented the whole awkward leap in a video called "PC FanBoy Switches to NEW MacBook Pro - Should You?" . Learning macOS as a complete noob was painful for several weeks, and it didn't really click until a few months later. But when it finally did, I got why creators love these things. Five years later, it's the longest I've ever gone without "needing" a new laptop. It was one of my most expensive purchases at the time, but looking back all these years, probably one of the best investments I've ever made, despite how sad it made my bank statement look. Since joining the Tom's Guide video team, my DaVinci Resolve projects have become far more demanding, with easily 8+ layers and several heavy GPU effects running at once. That finally caught up with my 5-year-old M1 Max, which now wheezes like it just climbed 10 flights of stairs. Every new MacBook Pro since has looked appealing, and I won't lie, I've had a few Apple shopping carts configured, but I never found it in me to hit that checkout button. Then Apple announced the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR Display , and three things caught my eye: a tandem OLED screen (two OLED layers stacked for more brightness), a lighter body, and a touchscreen. Touch was the big keynote moment, but everything else made me ready to upgrade. What 5 years of upgrades look like for me (Image credit: Tom's Guide) For the past two weeks, I've edited exclusively on the 16-inch MacBook Pro OLED in the M5 Max, 128GB, nano-texture configuration. Here's what the jump from my old 14-inch M1 Max with 32GB looks like. The chip goes from M1 Max to M5 Max, and the memory quadruples. The screen grows from 14 inches to 16. I've wished for that bigger screen for years, but I always talked myself out of a 16-inch because of the weight. This one weighs 4.1 pounds, about 0.6 pounds less than the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro. My M1 Max is around 3.5 pounds, so for roughly 0.6 pounds more I get a much bigger display. It's the first time a 16-inch laptop felt worth it to me. The new screen is a big part of why: it's what makes the body lighter, thinner, and slightly smaller, even though the display is slightly larger than on the non-touch MacBook Pros. At 0.63 inches thick, it's a hair slimmer than the 0.66-inch non-touch model; the footprint is slightly smaller, and the display grows from 16.2 to 16.3 inches. Then there are ports. My M1 Max has Thunderbolt 4, and that's why my massive Dell 52-inch 6K monitor was always stuck at 60Hz. The new laptop has three Thunderbolt 5 ports (the faster version of the same USB-C connector), and my monitor finally runs at 144Hz. Wi-Fi also jumps to Wi-Fi 7 from the Wi-Fi 6 on my old Mac, giving me faster connectivity when I'm working on the go. And don't forget the return of the glowing Apple logo on the lid. The last MacBook Pro with one was back in 2015, so I only ever admired it from the outside, like the cool kids' lunch table. Sure, I never actually saw it glow, but I'm finally sitting at the table. The screen is the real reason (Image credit: Tom's Guide) But here's what's really important. This is the best laptop display I've ever tested. I ran the same video project on this and a non-OLED MacBook Pro, and the shadows and bright scenes make fine details and color editing more precise. Apple rates the panel at up to 2,000 nits, and our lab measured 1,949, the brightest laptop screen Tom's Guide has tested. The nano-texture glass is one of the most important choices you'll make here. It's an anti-glare finish that costs $150 extra, and while Apple has offered it before, it's especially worth it on a touchscreen. The surface feels smoother and more premium under your finger, while the standard glass feels more resistant by comparison. It also hides fingerprints better. It's also why I can finally work away from my desk. I never used to edit on the go or outside…

articles.title: Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China?
articles.content: In three years "Megaspeed International" went from from inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary "to one of Asia's biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US," reports CNN. "It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks," trade data investigator William George told CNN. As Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, "Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia," CNN writes, noting scrutiny of the company from the Singapore government and US officials "concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers..." In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia's most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China's tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them. US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those... [T]rade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia... Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year... Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company's server purchases and their final destinations. In a statement, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence that Huang had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information "to downplay her role" at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing. The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws. A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia. CNN reminds readers that Jensen Huang accompanied US President Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, and also lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. "The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue." "However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well," they add. And the Taiwanese government is even seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, "as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 50th Anniversary of 'Star Wars' Celebrated with iMax 70mm Re-Release, Special Events, New Movie
articles.content: "Lucasfilm and Disney have restored the original Star Wars (1977) and will release the film in multiple formats, including Imax 70mm [starting February 19], as part of the franchise's 50th anniversary celebrations," reports Deadline. The original film will also be displayed in its original 16:9 format on the center of Cosm's 12K+ LED Dome, in a special presentation developed with Disney, Lucasfilm, ILM, and MakeMake. They're calling it a "Shared Reality production" where "the surrounding visual environments dynamically evolve to immerse the audience in iconic Star Wars locations and moments." Deadline reports more 50th anniversary celebrations In addition to the Imax 70mm screenings, the film will also be presented in Digital Imax, Digital Cinema, 70mm, 35mm, and 4DX. On May 4th, 2027, Lucasfilm will release a new behind-the-scenes documentary, The Hero Awakens, from filmmaker R.J. Cutler on Disney+. Star Wars events already on the calendar for 2027 include Shawn Levy's [movie] Star Wars: Starfighter, which will be released May 28. There's also a new poster paying homage to the original 1977 film, reports the Disney news site Mickey Visit, plus a newly orchestrated score by John Williams that they assume "will be used on all the projects that debut this year." On April 2-3, [Disney] will debut the new "Star Wars in Concert: The Skywalker Saga" at the Hollywood Bowl. The show will be hosted by Anthony Daniels, known for his role as C-3PO. Special performances of John Williams' iconic film scores will feature scenes and music from all nine Skywalker Saga films. The concert is a sweeping celebration of the stories, themes, and music that have inspired audiences around the world for five decades... They also teased that new and legacy licensees — including Hasbro, the LEGO Group, adidas, Mars, Aston Martin, Steinway, Hajime Sorayama presented by Complex, and more — will introduce 50th-anniversary collections... In the opening of the press release, Disney mentioned that as part of the announcements there will be "reimagined Disney Parks and Cruise Line offerings." The article adds that the April's Star Wars Celebration at the Los Angeles Convention Center has already sold out. There's more Star Wars news, writes long-time Slashdot reader schwit1 A light saber used by Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction. The light saber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City in which Vader tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father" sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, according to the auction house. The previous record was Heritage's $3,750,000 sale of Luke Skywalker's lightsaber and severed hand effects rig on July 15, 2026. And they're still auctioning more Star Wars memorabilia... Read more of this story at Slashdot.
