articles.title: Rainbow Six Siege Year 11 Season 4 sees the return of a largely forgotten healer and a host of welcome changes to the UI and ranked ecosystem — here's everything you need to know
articles.content: If you tuned in to the Rainbow Six Siege Osaka majors this weekend, you’ll have noticed that a long-sidelined operator took center stage — Doc. As 20 teams duked it out in front of a screaming crowd, competing to earn $200,000 in prize money, the trophy they were coveting was shaped in the likeness of the healer-focused operator. As palpable tension rippled through the packed ATC hall, moments before the tournament’s final, we soon discovered why. A pre-Finals panel revealed that in Season 4, the largely forgotten healing character will be getting a huge revamp. Instead of shooting direct stim pistol darts from afar, Doc will now be armed with a brand new gadget — the E-HEAL Monitor system. Using the E-HEAL, Doc will be able to remotely heal and — even revive — teammates from across the map (including through walls). (Image credit: Ubisoft) It turns out, it's a good time to be a support player, because the Doc isn't the only healer-focused update coming next season. Operator Thunderbird is also coming back in a big way, with her Kóna Stations receiving a significant buff. Her number of Kóna Stations will be increased from 3 to 4 for broader site coverage, and if that wasn't enough to make you consider her, she’ll receive a new weapon too: the MBZ-19. Thunderbirds really are go. Alongside these intriguing operator remasters, an FPS legend is joining the fray — the Doom Slayer. In this surprise collaboration with Doom, the iconic anti-hero will become a part of Siege on December 22 in skin form — and you can read more about that here . A drastic UI overhaul (Image credit: Ubisoft) The beloved map Bank has also had an update that seeks to level the playing field between attackers and defenders. Adding a new access point and exterior cover around the entry point, Ubisoft Montreal says they're aiming to rebalance a map that's currently weighted too heavily in the defenders' favour. A new temporary testing ground will also allow the community to weigh in on a potential new secondary gadget which allows defenders to reinforce just part of a wall, leaving the rest open for lines of sight. Yet for hardcore fans, some of the most welcome changes will be the least exciting on paper. For year 11 and season 4, Rainbow Six Siege 's UI has undergone a drastic overhaul, and with it, new types of matchmaking have been introduced. The Ranked ecosystem is getting an overhaul, splitting the competitive mode into dedicated Ranked Solo/Duo and Ranked Flex playlists. The aim is to keep individual and duo players from clashing with larger, coordinated squads, hopefully saving some frustration and heartache for solo players. This will work in conjunction with Cross-Queue Matchmaking, in a bid to keep those match queue times fast. Additionally, the level requirement to unlock Ranked will be dropping from 50 to 30, helping newer players to jump in sooner. Ranked playlist alterations are finally here (Image credit: Ubisoft) “The solo/duo ranked playlist is something that we've been trying to do for years,” beams Rainbow Six Siege Game Director Chris Budgens, "We've always gotten cold feet, so we started looking at how we actually pull off a solo queue within Siege, while respecting healthy queue times and so on. Every time we tried to do it, we would get scared by the data — this might be a bit more destructive than we're ready to deal with at the moment because we had other known quantities such as Rank 3.0 we wanted to work on.” “We had so much data support in terms of our analysts and simulations and matchmaking queue times, and finally cracked it,” he adds. “We're really happy to be able to bring that to players because they've been asking for years to have a solo queue playlist.” Alongside new ranking queues, playing with your friends promises to be markedly less of a pain in the backside. An all-new Social Hub consolidates Ubisoft Connect and first-party platform friends into a single list, aiming to offer cleaner and less intrusive notifications.…

articles.title: 'You can't just take any IP character and throw them in because it just doesn't work. That's where skin collaborations work' — The Doom Slayer is the latest gaming icon to join Rainbow Six Siege and will be fragging his way onto Season 4
articles.content: Doom’s iconic anti-hero is ripping and tearing his way into Rainbow Six Siege. Taking to the stage in Osaka during Rainbow Six Siege ’s 2026 Majors tournament, Creative Director Joshua Mills revealed that the legendary first-person shooter (FPS) protagonist will be fragging his way into Siege as a new skin for Tachanka. Heading to the game on December 22, players will get a chance to rip and tear their way across the Siege universe as part of the game’s long-awaited fourth season. While the Doom Slayer’s in-game skin has yet to be revealed, his appearance was teased via a short video. As a portal to hell opens into the biker gang compound map Clubhouse, the Doom Slayer blasts a moving Rainbow Six drone before Mick Gordon’s signature guitar riff kicks in. The Doom Slayer skin comes after a wave of recent similar collaborations, with everything from Halo , Resident Evil , and Tomb Raider skins making appearances in Ubisoft’s FPS. “Doom means so much to me personally, and for many on the team that played Doom as kids growing up,” says Game Director Chris Budgens. “I think that skins are the best way [to implement most collaborations]. With skins, we get a lot more leeway in terms of having fun with the characters and franchises. To date, Rainbow Six Siege has only one permanent canon playable operator from a different fictional universe — Metal Gear Solid ’s Solid Snake — and as The Doom Slayer joins as a skin, it appears that Ubisoft Montreal wants to keep it that way for now. “We don't want to just flood the game with different partners,” reflects Budgens. “It has to be right.” Re-imagining icons (Image credit: Ubisoft) Snake’s inclusion, it seems, has been well judged. Since Solid Snake’s surprise introduction to Siege in March 2026, he’s become a beloved character in the game, slotting into Siege’s more grounded fictional universe with surprising ease. As I sit backstage at the Osaka 2026 majors, Ubisoft Montreal tells me that Solid Snake’s inclusion was an IP infiltration years in the making. “We had originally brought up the idea, and [Konami] were interested right from the get-go,” reveals Budgens. “One of the funny things was, what does this actually look like? Are we going with a skin? We had some interest in bringing Solid Snake as the operator into the game, but we had never really done that before—an operator from another franchise.” Creative director Joshua Mills, however, needed a bit more convincing that Snake would work in Siege’s gritty, grounded universe. “Alex Karpazis, the previous creative director, brought the idea to me and said, 'Listen, I want to bring [Snake] into the game, and I was like, 'You want to do what? How's that going to work?'” recalls Mills, “'If you say the cardboard box, I'm walking away right now!” In order to make Snake work alongside Sam Fisher and alongside SWAT team-esque operators, they decided to reimagine Snake as a Tom Clancy-esque agent. “We came up with a very clear rationale, which was: it's Solid Snake as if he existed within the Rainbow Six universe,” recalls Mills. “It allows us to take everything that's iconic about the character and make it more grounded and canon in Rainbow Six …. Then we got to make that legendary pairing with Snake and Zero [Sam Fisher], an opportunity of a lifetime to be able to do that.” Where the Doom Slayer is very much a classic skin-based collaboration, Mills suggests that The Boss’ inclusion in Rainbow Six Siege has opened the door to future fully fledged third-party operators. “We've definitely talked about other collaborations for a canon-based operator,” teases Mills. "We're very, very strict about who we would work with on this and who we would bring in because, again, we have to rationalise it one way or another. You can't just take any IP character and throw them in because it just doesn't work. That's where skin collaborations work fine… [but for operators ] There are some ideas, but nothing to confirm at the moment." You can read more…

articles.title: Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation
articles.content: October 3: $84,680 Today: $64,108 Bitcoin dropped 24.2% in 46 days. And it "fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500," reports Fortune, "wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over." The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm's demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again. The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether's USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets. This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday's Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase. "Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise... people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find... government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income," Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune... Heavy borrowing and spending on AI have created what 21Shares calls an "AI black hole," drawing money toward the sector and away from assets like Bitcoin and gold. But Bitcoin remains "joined at the hip" with tech stocks, according to Beauchamp. That leaves it in an awkward position: It faces competition for investment dollars when enthusiasm for AI runs high, yet can get dragged down when that enthusiasm fades. Fast Company points out Bitcoin "remains down more than 20% since the beginning of 2026." [Nvidia] has seen its shares lose more than 27% of their value over the past month. The tech sell-off seems to have dragged down the crypto markets, too, as the two sectors are, on some levels, intermingled... On top of that, outflows from Bitcoin funds may also be contributing to the slide. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were closed in recent days, which may have added to declining demand, affecting BTC prices. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: With Starship catch, SpaceX still shows it can dazzle the world
articles.content: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

articles.title: America Officially Loses Its Measles-elimination Status After Continued Spread of the Disease
articles.content: Reuters reports: The Pan American Health Organization has revoked the United States' measles-elimination status, ending a 26-year run after determining the country failed to halt continuous transmission of the highly contagious virus for more than a year, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday... The reported decision by the Americas branch of the World Health Organization comes as the US battles the highest number of measles cases it has seen in more than three decades. Some 7,500 people in the US have been infected with measles and 13 have died since 2025. That period coincides with falling immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines... Canada, Spain and the UK recently lost measles-elimination status after review by WHO experts.... "It is a fully preventable disease. It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles," said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina... William Moss, an epidemiology professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said loss of measles elimination was a hit to the United States' reputation as a public health powerhouse... For the average American, he added, it means that the United States will continue to have large outbreaks, putting people at risk of disease, hospitalization and death. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Manjaro Linux Moves Toward Independent Community Governance
articles.content: Arch-based Manjaro Linux "has announced that Manjaro Project e.V. is now officially registered as a non-profit in Germany," reports Linuxiac, "and is therefore a legally separate entity from the commercial Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG... after months of internal wrangling over who was in charge of the project, who had access to the infrastructure and who didn't, and the relationship between the dev team and the commercial company..." The restructuring goes back to March, when the Manjaro developers released the Manjaro 2.0 Manifesto, which was a very public critique of the way Manjaro was being run. The document claims that decision-making has effectively become the sole domain of the project founder, Philip Müller, with the other developers having very limited access to the infrastructure. There's also a concern about the drop in participation, the persistent technical issues, and the continued prioritization of commercial interests over the actual development of the distribution... The manifesto proposed the transfer of all project infrastructure, domains, repositories and community funds to the new organization, together with arrangements for the use of the Manjaro trademark. The contributors were warning that they might well consider forking the distro if the talks didn't go their way. Müller then indicated that he'd be happy to talk about the proposed structure once the non-profit was in place. The association is now formally registered, and so one of the key aims of the manifesto has been realized... Perhaps the most important point is the actual evolution of the distribution. The most recent testing and stable updates were kicked off by the Manjaro team themselves, without any oversight from Müller. This points to the developers having already started to operate on their own in an area which was previously the preserve of the project's founder. They're also in the process of optimizing their dev infrastructure, in part as a response to the continued automated bot attacks on the existing infrastructure. Thanks to Slashdot reader king*jojo for sharing the news. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not
articles.content: Jensen Huang, top left, and 11 executives mentioned in this story as possible successors. Top row, from left: Huang, Rene Haas, Colette Kress and Ian Buck. Middle: Lisa Su, Thomas Kurian, Peter DeSantis and Dave Treadwell. Bottom: Amy Hood, Matt Garman, Judson Althoff and Nick Parker. (Company and LinkedIn Photos) Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names. The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday. Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy. Colette Kress , the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career. Others would rather have Huang back. Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang. The organizers of one, called “ Stand with Jensen ,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees. The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment. Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU , paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs. Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported. He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013. Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.” One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi , SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia. He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis. John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s…
articles.author: Todd Bishop

articles.title: Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
articles.content: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15's booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its "Mechazilla" launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ' chopstick ' catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company's third-quarter earnings call that "success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight." articles.title: EFF Criticizes US Government's Use of AI For Evaluating Senior Health Insurance Requests
articles.content: "When we need medical care, we expect decisions about our treatment to be made by our doctors, not a tech company's algorithm," writes the EFF newsletter EFFector. But in January America's federal government launched a program called WISeR that uses AI to evaluate authorization requests for certain procedures from America's federal health insurance program for seniors, Medicare. EFF sued for records and discovered "additional issues" with the program that they say "could jeopardize Medicare beneficiaries' access to care." The records we received revealed that WISeR has resulted in widespread delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Further documents obtained by EFF show a rushed and rocky rollout, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments treat AI like a silver bullet for complex problems. EFF has now published hundreds of pages of documents obtained through our lawsuit, available here... The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. EFF has long argued that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples' rights or access to benefits, such as immigration enforcement and policing decisions. That's because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people's rights or deprive them of benefits they're entitled to based on biased or inappropriate considerations and without proper due process or accountability if there is an error. By outsourcing decision-making to private AI companies without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits, WISeR jeopardizes seniors' access to medical care. Congress should step in to place greater legal limits on the use of automated decision-making in Medicare. The new documents "show why we need stronger legal limits around government use of automated decision-making..." according to the newsletter. And another EFF page argues that the American public "still lacks the information needed to assess whether clinician review is providing meaningful oversight of AI systems and whether appropriate data is being used to evaluate prior authorization requests." WISeR's payment structure gives vendors, as the government put it, "an incentive to deny as many claims as possible...." [One company] denied more requests than it approved in the first few months of the program, and CMS inquired about "denials that appear inaccurate or inconsistent with applicable criteria." Ultimately, the records obtained by EFF raise more questions than they answer about the safeguards used by WISeR vendors... A growing body of scholarship points to the substantial limitations of "human in the loop" policies as guardrails for AI systems. AI-generated recommendations can unduly influence human decisions, leading reviewers to over-rely on automated judgements and rubber stamp them as correct. Even worse, at least one health insurance company actively pressured clinical reviewers to accept its AI systems' recommendations. Another company built a system that allowed clinical reviewers to reject claims without opening patient files; clinical reviewers using this system spent an average of just 1.2 seconds on each case.. As the government expands its use of automated decision-making, the potential for consequential mistakes increases rapidly. The records we've obtained so far raise questions about the rushed rollout and lack of guardrails for automated decision-making by the U.S. government. EFF urges transparency, oversight, and legal limits to protect people from the harms of automated decision-making in high risk systems. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Hundreds of Fake Accounts Defended Jensen Huang On Social Media
articles.content: The Washington Post reports on something peculiar about support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang online after he'd told the world he'd been unfaithful to his wife (before reports of his second extramarital affair): Joining the chorus online were voices of seemingly everyday people: a chef, a stock trader, a Hebrew teacher and several environmental activists. But at least 400 of them were fake, according to research from the nonprofit Midas Project, with links to a public relations firm involved in previous so-called "sockpuppet" campaigns... Many of the fake accounts, according to Midas Project executive director Tyler Johnston, replied to journalists, former U.S. officials and other prominent figures and backed not just Huang but Nvidia's push to sell its cutting-edge chips to Chinese firms. Like other documented influence campaigns, the posts appeared to have limited reach; the most-viewed tweet garnered about 8,000 views and 32 likes. Still, some of the posts targeted lawmakers, including accounts for the [U.S.] House Select Committee on China, Republicans on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts). "That's a place where you might not need a lot of views, but maybe the staffers who are running the lawmakers' account are paying attention to how their messages are received," said Johnston, whose group advocates for safe AI development... There were other clues that helped identify accounts as being part of an apparently coordinated campaign, according to the Midas Project. Some of them were created minutes or hours apart, and had user names and profile photos refreshed at similar times. They also sometimes engaged on oddly specific issues ranging from Qatar to Nippon Steel's bid for U.S. Steel and a waste management plant in Oregon.... Any one one of the posts — often replies to other posts — might have not looked suspicious in isolation. But the various clues taken together, Johnston said, gave evidence that they were linked. Some of the accounts then rushed to delete posts after he posted his findings online, and at least 260 of them have been deactivated or suspended by X. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
articles.content: "It's really happening. I promise. For real." Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering , in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker , the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027. An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. articles.title: Why Your NumPy Array Changed After Preprocessing (Views vs Copies in ML)
articles.content: A small NumPy operation can modify data you never intended to touch. Understanding views, copies, and memory sharing can prevent silent bugs in machine learning pipelines. Introduction Imagine preparing a dataset for a machine learning model. You load the original data, select a few columns, normalize their values, and pass the result to your training algorithm. Everything appears to work correctly. Later, when you inspect the original dataset, something looks wrong. Some values have changed, even though you never directly modified the original array. This is one of those Python behaviors that can make debugging surprisingly difficult. The problem usually comes down to how NumPy handles memory. When you create a new array from an existing one, NumPy does not always allocate new memory. Sometimes, it creates a view that points to the same underlying data. This matters most during preprocessing, where slicing, normalization, reshaping, and feature selection are common. Let’s look at why it happens, how to detect it, and how to avoid it. 1. The Difference Between a NumPy View and a Copy A view creates a new array object that shares memory with another array. A copy creates a separate array with its own data. import numpy as np original = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]) view = original[1:4] view[0] = 999 print("Original:", original) print("View:", view) Output: Original: [ 10 999 30 40 50] View: [999 30 40] The original array changed even though we modified only the view variable. Basic slicing creates a view, so both arrays reference the same memory for the selected elements. Now, the same operation with .copy() : original = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]) copied = original[1:4].copy() copied[0] = 999 print("Original:", original) print("Copy:", copied) Output: Original: [10 20 30 40 50] Copy: [999 30 40] The original array is unchanged. The difference isn’t in the variable names or values. It’s in how NumPy manages memory. If you’ve seen the same idea with plain Python lists, see Why .copy() in Python Still Mutates Your Original List. 2. Why This Becomes a Problem During ML Preprocessing Machine learning preprocessing often involves selecting features and transforming numerical values. import numpy as np data = np.array([ [100, 20, 5], [200, 30, 10], [300, 40, 15], [400, 50, 20] ], dtype=float) Suppose the first two columns are features you want to center around zero. A developer might write: features = data[:, :2] features -= features.mean(axis=0) print(features) print(data) The features look correct: [[ -150. -15.] [ -50. -5.] [ 50. 5.] [ 150. 15.]] But the original dataset has also changed: [[-150. -15. 5.] [ -50. -5. 10.] [ 50. 5. 15.] [ 150. 15. 20.]] The cause is this line: features = data[:, :2] Slicing created a view of data . Then features -= ... modified the values in place, and since features and data share memory, the change appeared in both. This is especially dangerous when the original dataset is needed for another preprocessing step, a model comparison, or evaluation. 3. The Fix: Create an Independent Copy Before Preprocessing Instead of: features = data[:, :2] use: features = data[:, :2].copy() features -= features.mean(axis=0) print("Processed features:") print(features) print("Original dataset:") print(data) The processed features are transformed, and the original dataset stays intact. This .copy() call makes the intent explicit: the preprocessing should work on independent data. Copying everything is not always necessary, though, because it increases memory usage, especially with large datasets. The better habit is knowing when NumPy shares memory and when it doesn’t. 4. How to Check Whether Two Arrays Share Memory NumPy provides np.shares_memory() for this: import numpy as np original = np.arange(10) view = original[2:7] copied = original[2:7].copy() print(np.shares_memory(original, view)) print(np.shares_memory(original, copied)) Output: True False You can also inspect the .base attribute: print(view.base is…

articles.title: ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox
articles.content: Microsoft says it has restored service after a Microsoft 365 outage cut off email in more than 70 countries. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted. “Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group. Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote . Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details. Related ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log . Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal. A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online. He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user , he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five. In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud. Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth. Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto , a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments ; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption. In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported , citing Nikkei. In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems , including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email. About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear . Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.” Microsoft itself looked…

articles.title: My Local AI Agent Needed a Bigger Brain, So I Gave It a Decentralized GPU
articles.content: this is my second progress update for the Decentralize AI Hackathon by HackerNoon and Nosana. In my first article, I Built a Local AI Linux Assistant That Doesn't Rely on the Cloud , I introduced zkzkAgent: an AI agent that manages a Linux machine through plain language and runs entirely on my own hardware with Ollama. That is still how it works by default. But running everything locally has a ceiling, and I kept hitting it. The Problem: The Model That Fits on a Laptop zkzkAgent doesn't push every request through one big prompt. A small classifier node first decides what kind of request it is: a question to answer, a single action to run, or a task that needs a plan. Plans are where the agent is most useful, and they are also where the model works hardest. To scaffold a project, the planner writes every step, including the full content of every file, before anything runs. On my laptop, I run a 2B model ( qwen3.5:2b ). It fits in memory and answers quickly. A 27B model does not fit. Until now, anyone on modest hardware had two options: accept a small model, or send everything to a centralized AI provider. Nosana adds a third option: rent a GPU from a decentralized network, only for the model, and keep everything else at home. zkzkAgent in 30 Seconds A multi-node LangGraph graph . Separate nodes classify the request, answer questions, write plans, and execute tools. The router logs every decision with the reason for it. 25 tools for files, apps, networking, processes, packages, and deployment. Human-in-the-loop safety . Destructive tools (removing files, emptying the trash, installing or removing packages) are blocked in code until I type yes . A chat CLI with live streaming, history and slash commands, plus Docker support and an optional voice mode. The Design Rule: Only the Model Moves Before writing any code, I set one rule for the integration: Nosana gets the model calls and nothing else. The graph, the routing, the confirmation gates, and all 25 tools still run on my machine. A model on a remote GPU can suggest remove_file . Only my machine can run it, and only after I type yes . That rule kept the change small. It lives in one file, models/LLM.py , and it is controlled by one setting in `.env`: MODEL_TYPE="NOSANA" NOSANA_API_KEY="nos_..." NOSANA_BASE_URL="https://inference.nosana.com/v1" NOSANA_MODEL="qwen/qwen3.8-27b" Nosana's inference API uses the OpenAI chat format, so the agent talks to it through LangChain's `ChatOpenAI` client. The rest of the graph only sees an `llm` object and doesn't know which backend is behind it: if MODEL_TYPE == "NOSANA": API_KEY = _env("NOSANA_API_KEY") if not API_KEY.startswith("nos_"): raise RuntimeError("NOSANA_API_KEY missing or invalid (must start with 'nos_').") BASE_URL = _env("NOSANA_BASE_URL", NOSANA_URL).rstrip("/") MODEL_NAME = _env("NOSANA_MODEL") or _pick_nosana_model(BASE_URL, API_KEY) llm = ChatOpenAI( model=MODEL_NAME, base_url=BASE_URL, api_key=API_KEY, timeout=120, max_retries=2, stream_usage=True, # final chunk carries token counts ) elif MODEL_TYPE == "OLLAMA": pass #the other implement of the code Three details are worth explaining: Picking a live model. On Nosana, a model only appears in GET /models while a GPU is actually serving it. If `NOSANA_MODEL` is empty, the agent fetches that list and uses the first available model, so it never starts against a model that nobody is serving. Token counts . With stream_usage=True , the last streamed chunk includes token usage. That is what usage is billed on, and it is the basis for the cost numbers I plan to publish next. Bring your own GPU job. The repo also includes nosana-ollama.json , a Nosana job definition that starts the official Ollama container on a GPU node and pulls qwen3:14b . It is for people who want their own model server on Nosana instead of the shared API. Case Study: One Request, One Working Web App To test the integration in real work, I switched to the 27B model on Nosana and gave zkzkAgent a task: create a…

articles.title: AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part.
articles.content: This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It covers more than 200 AWS services and was written entirely by agents. The most useful part of the launch is a story Swami Sivasubramanian tells in the announcement. About 20 years ago, Sivasubramanian helped build the replication engine inside Alf, a Paxos-based lock service that still powers AWS systems such as S3 and DynamoDB. The first build took about four months. When he later asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to rebuild it, he supervised the agent for four nights before he saw the problem: The agent had no way to check its own results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours. Same agent, same task. Four nights became two hours because the feedback loop changed. “An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against.” As Sivasubramanian puts it, distributed systems are hard to test. That matches what I see across teams running coding agents on production systems. An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against. AWS Emulator solves that for the AWS APIs your code calls. It does not solve it for the services your team owns, and that is where most agent-written changes break. AWS puts infrastructure inside the agent’s loop A coding agent works in a loop. It writes code, runs it, reads the result, and decides what to change next. Sivasubramanian’s point is that in distributed systems, that loop runs inside infrastructure. If the services the code calls do not behave like the real ones, the agent learns the wrong lesson and keeps going. AWS Emulator puts AWS into that loop on a laptop. Point existing AWS tools and code at it with one environment variable, and tests run against emulated services without changes. Autonomous agents wrote every line of the emulator, working from AWS’s public API models. Each behavior is pinned by a fidelity test that first passes against real AWS, then against the emulator, and every change passes a merge gate where security agents review it. Sivasubramanian’s conclusion is that when agents write the code, the engineer’s job is to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when the work is correct. The first reactions on Hacker News went straight to trust. One commenter counted roughly 30,000 commits in three weeks and questioned the quality. That is a fair question aimed at the wrong thing. Who wrote the code tells you little. What it was verified against tells you a lot, and AWS’s answer is real AWS. “Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.” What changed is who runs the loop. A developer checks a change a few times a day, and an agent checks it on every iteration. Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all. Every loop runs against mocks, an emulator, or the running system An agent can verify its work against one of three things, and each has a different weakness. Mocks are the weakest option, and AI has made them cheap. One Hacker News commenter argued that it is now faster to have AI mock your APIs , adding that “AI has been a boon for test coverage.” But an agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not. Emulators are a real step up. AWS Emulator is checked against real AWS, so its behavior comes from the service rather than from the agent. An emulator is still a model, though, and AWS is open about that. The repository keeps a folder of behaviors the agents found that do not match real AWS yet, and operations that are not implemented return an error instead of a fake success. An IDC…

articles.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix
articles.content: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our head-to-head coding comparisons. Anthropic compared Fable 5.2 with its predecessor, Fable 5.1 , on safeguard blocks, output speed, and API pricing. The company states that Fable 5.2 triggered about 55% fewer safeguard blocks than Fable 5.1 overall and about 60% fewer in cybersecurity in early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork. It also says Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster and lists standard API rates of $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Both rates are 20% lower than Fable 5.1’s $10 and $50. I compared Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1 on three developer tasks and tracked refusals, accuracy, tokens, estimated cost, and elapsed time. The comparison uses one run per model for each task or version, including the October Fable 5.1 webhook result. That’s a small sample, and the API runs used a different setup from Anthropic’s safeguard testing. The tests For the new runs, I used Anthropic’s API with the default effort setting of High for both models, with no turn cap or fallback model. A script graded every run against an answer key I created for the tests. The dollar figures are estimated API costs. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately . Webhook chat : I reused a 50-turn scripted chat that I first ran on Fable 5.1 in October. It simulates a dev lead building a small webhook relay. The chat contains 25 project rules, eight of which change later and three of which are only implied. At the end, the model writes the config and code and then takes an eight-question recall quiz. Signature checker : I gave each model a written spec for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders, and then sent a change request. A hidden suite of 50 tests graded the final code output. Login repo fix : Each model worked as an agent in a small login library with interacting bugs in passwords, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit. Webhook chat In the October Fable 5.1 run I’m using for comparison, the API refused 34 of 50 turns. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. In that October run, I kept my prompts in the chat history and discarded refused model responses. Fable 5.1 also refused the final code and the quiz, so it scored zero on both. The task was to build an ordinary backend relay. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. Fable 5.2 finished the same script without a refusal. That gave me a complete run to grade for long-conversation recall. Its code used the most recent version of all eight rules, which changed midway, and on the quiz it answered “unknown” to the three questions that had no answer. Fable 5.2 didn’t fill gaps with guesses. The numbers: • Fable 5.2 : 50 turns, 298,709 in, 41,828 out (28,550 reasoning), $4.06, 427 s. • Fable 5.1 (October) : 34 of 50 turns refused, with no code or quiz answers. Signature checker Fable 5.1 refused both turns of this test in under a second each, and the API labeled both refusals “cyber.” The spec asked for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders. The API returned no output on either turn. Anthropic says benign security work can trigger its cyber classifier . Fable 5.2 took the same spec, handled the change request, and passed all 50 hidden tests, including the edge cases on timestamps, rotated secrets, and replays. The numbers: Fable 5.2 : 2 turns, 21,299 in, 26,167 out (18,407 reasoning), $1.22, 253 s. Fable 5.1 : 2 turns, both refused, 3,206 reported input tokens, 0 output tokens, $0.00 under Anthropic’s billing rules for cyber refusals before output , 2 s. Login repo fix This was…

articles.title: Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy
articles.content: Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer ( WeightSpace ) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp , needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. How is it different from fine-tuning or prompt optimization? It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull: Prompt optimization (DSPy’s MIPROv2, GEPA ) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change. Fine-tuning (DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside BetterTogether ) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU. Weight-space programming changes weights by reasoning. The editor forms a hypothesis (“these neurons over-score option B”), writes code to patch them, and checks the result with a few forward passes. The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly. What did the original research show? The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking: Reading weights: Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone. Fixing a broken policy: A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes. Writing from zero: On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps. Fixing an LLM: Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability. How does dspy-wsp…

articles.title: Samsung's 1TB 990 SSD drops to 19 cents per GB amid the memory crisis — grab it for $40 off
articles.content: Getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging. That said, the Samsung 990 SSD is currently available at a discounted price of $189.99 , against its original list price of $229.99 on Amazon. Although the $40 saving might not seem that impressive, deals on high-performance internal SSDs are becoming harder to come by amid the ongoing NAND and DRAM crisis. If you've been holding off on a storage upgrade, this could be a good opportunity to pick up a reliable, high-speed SSD. Check out this deal on Amazon The Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller. It was introduced earlier this year with MSRPs of $269.99 for the 1TB model and $529.99 for the 2TB model. The 1TB model offers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and 6,450 MB/s, making it an excellent option for everyday computing, gaming, and handling large files. Samsung rates the drive for up to 400TB of written data, although it offers just three years of warranty. It features a single-sided M.2 2280 design, which should make it compatible with a wide range of desktop motherboards, laptops, and even mini-PCs. 990 1TB: was $229.99 now $189.99 Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications. View Deal In our testing of the 2TB variant , we found that the Samsung 990 delivers reasonably good all-around performance, particularly for gaming and everyday applications. It offered similar performance to the Samsung 990 EVO Plus in some tests. However, it fell behind competing drives such as the Crucial P310 and WD Blue SN5100 in others, particularly during file transfers. One of its biggest advantages is its large write cache, which allows it to maintain speeds of nearly 6,100 MB/s for more than 57 seconds before performance drops once the cache is exhausted. Its power efficiency may not be the best, but overall it is a competent budget PCIe 4.0 SSD. Samsung Samsung Samsung For anyone upgrading from an older SATA SSD or a traditional hard drive, the Samsung 990 should offer a noticeable improvement in boot times, application loading, and overall system responsiveness. At its current price of $189.99 , it is also a suitable option for expanding game storage without spending a fortune.

articles.content: This week on the GeekWire Podcast, we react to the sudden downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose resignation Nvidia announced Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Inspired by Colette Kress’s new role, the GeekWire Trivia Challenge looks at what some of Microsoft’s former finance executives have done after leaving the company. articles.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
articles.content: AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth , try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training. “Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.” Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess. This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer. The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools. Web results Internal data Freshness Often hours or days old Can be months out of date without anyone noticing Quality Uneven: official docs next to forum threads Curated, but written for a past state of the product Structure Mostly unstructured text Mix of text, metadata and structured records Authority Has to be inferred from the source Known, but rarely stored as a field Access control Public Per customer, region, contract or role The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it? Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available. Why concatenating results breaks in production The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways: Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither. Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date. Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones. Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers. A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. articles.title: This week in Tom's Hardware Premium: November 14, 2026 — Mac Studio versus DGX Spark, AMD's MEXT cuts DRAM requirements in half, and the Huang saga reaches critical mass
articles.content: Seismic appears to set the tone for this week's events in the hardware industry, and we've covered the biggest beats, including deeper dives on hardware and AI topics over on Tom's Hardware Premium . Stories this week are colored by the fact that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has stepped away from his post as CEO. The ramifications are wide and far-reaching, as the company transformed from a gaming GPU manufacturer to an AI business over the past five years. First up, it's not only hyperscalers and neoclouds that have their eyes on AI. An increasingly popular segment among enthusiasts is PCs dedicated to running local AI models. With so many choices on the market currently, from the recently released RTX Spark to AMD's Strix Halo platform, we take a look at two unlikely contenders that are now going head-to-head: Nvidia's DGX Spark and Apple's Mac Studio. We ran a suite of real-world and synthetic benchmarks across both devices and tested large models on both machines. With prices at eye-watering levels, it's more crucial than ever that you make the correct choice for your intended workloads. Going deep on local AI performance benchmarking with Apple’s Mac Studio with M5 Ultra taking on Nvidia DGX Spark — inference engine recipes mandatory for bigger models as MLX stack matures DRAM capacity constraints have been an industry-wide sticking point as the AI buildout accelerates demand for dies. With costs spiraling across both client and enterprise hardware, AMD has shared further detail about MEXT, a predictive memory engine which aims to offer 99% of a server's performance while running on half the DRAM. Powered by a transformer model and clever use of flash storage, AMD is already running 145 servers with the system in place, with a view to expand that figure to 2,000 next year. AMD shares how it can retain 95% of server performance with just half the DRAM, sidestepping memory shortages with MEXT — tech powers over 100 servers already running, with plans to expand to 2,000 servers in 2027 Next, we sat down with Cognichip's Chief Product Officer in an extensive interview to explore how the company is rolling out AI-powered chip design tools. Back in September, the company revealed a suite of proprietary AI models, named Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), which are specifically developed for semiconductor engineering. While the tools have yet to be used in a shipping product, it could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks. Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Jensen Huang scandal deepens, as the now-former Nvidia CEO has become embroiled in a series of alleged extramarital affairs and has since resigned from Nvidia. While much of the past week's stories have centered on his relationship with alleged Chinese Spy Alice Huang, we explored the former CEO's unlikely relationship with Kang Wei, Ms. Huang's husband, who recently landed in hot water with China's Securities Regulatory Commission. How Shanghai fund manager Kang Wei introduced his wife Alice Huang to Jensen and built a $7.5 billion Nvidia AI GPU smuggling operation — Mistress's husband joked she was the Nvidia CEO's 'personal assistant' Nvidia-based compute remains difficult to find in China, especially as AI labs line up to order racks and newer cards like the RTX 5500 Pro, with over 6 million units reportedly ordered for the export-compliant GB202-based AI accelerator. But the Chinese AI labs that are chasing after Nvidia's tech may still have to pay a premium and ensure that they're running enough homegrown silicon to not fall afoul of Beijing's rules. We explore how some companies have now moved to renting compute in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore in an attempt to get around export controls. Nvidia cracks down on…

articles.title: DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
articles.content: How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the question in this episode of The New Stack podcast. DuckLake is an open-source table lakehouse format created by Amsterdam-based DuckLabs that acts as a traffic cop for data management by storing table metadata inside a standard SQL database, rather than scattering manifest files across object storage. Unlike traditional table formats, DuckLake treats lakehouse metadata as a relational database problem. These advanced data lake features, served by Parquet files and SQL databases, reduce the traditional lakehouse complexity. In October, DuckLake 1.1 launched alongside DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS . The New Stack sat down with Pedro Holanda , lead DuckLake developer and principal engineer at DuckLabs at their Amsterdam headquarters, to talk about the launch. Holanda has contributed to the DuckDB open-source project since it was an early research prototype, and shares the full evolution of DuckLake to our conversation. “These lakehouse formats exist so people can exchange their database systems without having to do migrations,” Holanda tells The New Stack . Because of the complexity, “you need a database system to keep track of which table has its last version.” DuckLake applies decades of research, Holanda says, in order to reduce files and therefore complexity at a time of rapid data growth, taking advantage of how everyone who uses database systems is familiar with SQL and how schemas work. “The simplicity is the way you fetch your data,” Holanda says of DuckLake. “You’re going to issue queries somewhere. The server is going to answer these questions back, and you know exactly which Parquet files you have to read. So the Parquet files don’t change. Just the catalog.” Maintainers of your data lake often have many maintenance tasks to perform. If you end up with many files, he says, DuckLake lets you glue them into one file to reduce the number of requests. This can also be done across multiple snapshots, further reducing the number of files. It also solves the “small files problem” in streaming data lakes and lakehouses by using inlining and flushing. Whereas for traditional data lakes, across multiple data sources being inserted at a time, “you end up with so many files, so when you have to query it, you’re going to have to traverse a bunch of metadata files just to figure out which Parquet files you need to read, and then you’re going to have a bunch of Parquet files to read as well,” Holanda says, slowing everything down and frustrating the developer. DuckLake is known to be fast, simple to use, and not requiring massive server clusters to run. Part of that comes from Parquet being very similar to DuckDB storage: both are columnar and organized in row groups, which keeps the massaging step to a minimum. “One thing that we realized when we were building DuckLake is that, ‘Hey, we have a database system now, we have a catalog; what if we do this radical idea of storing data on tables?'” he says. “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.” “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.” During Amazon’s Q3 earnings call in late October, CEO Andy Jassy called out the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines, especially as AWS customers’ data generation continues to increase. Amazon is famous for dogfooding, and Jassy pointed to DuckDB’s solution to this complexity as a reason for its DuckLabs acquisition . “With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS storage and analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and…

articles.title: U.S. Treasury Secretary questions whether Nvidia knowingly sold AI GPUs to shell companies, says company itself is responsible
articles.content: Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary, admitted that the U.S. export controls cannot prevent all the restricted hardware from reaching China or other adversaries, which is why the country allegedly obtained millions of restricted AI GPUs from Nvidia . At the same time, he questioned the efficiency of Nvidia's internal controls. called for accountability at Nvidia, criticized the company's general counsel, but stressed that it was unclear whether Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang knew about the potentially illicit practices. Go deeper with TH Premium: GPUs (Image credit: Noctua) Desktop GPU Roadmap Nvidia's Enterprise GPU Roadmap Testing DirectStorage with GPU decompression The GeForce RTX 30-series upgrade matrix — does your Ampere GPU need an upgrade in 2026? Rubin in-depth The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC "I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down," in an interview with CNBC (via @siliconmemes ). "One thing here is that the story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles. The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? And I think it is important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent admitted that despite strict U.S. export controls that prohibit sales of advanced AI GPUs to China, considerable quantities of restricted hardware may still make their way to the country. However, the Treasury Secretary does not believe that the U.S. needs to introduce more stringent export restrictions or grant government agencies additional powers to prevent GPU smuggling. Instead, the authorities should properly enforce existing regulations, according to Bessent. Bessent also criticized Nvidia's general counsel Timothy Teter, who reportedly contacted the U.S. Department of Commerce to inquire whether U.S. authorities were behind the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore. However, the Treasury Secretary declined to speculate about potential consequences for Nvidia if it turned out that some of its executives knew that their customers acted as intermediaries for Chinese entities. Meanwhile, Bessent expressed confidence that Nvidia's board of directors would conduct a thorough investigation into the matter. "But let us just say, if this was happening, then there were not robust controls at the company," Bessent said. "We do not know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this. The [general council] seems to have been very involved here, probably should have done more oversight rather than the haranguing [government officials at the U.S. DoC]." Bessent also revealed that the Departments of the Treasury, War, and State, as well as the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), had supported the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List for months. However, the authority to impose such export restrictions belongs to the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which reportedly stalled efforts to blacklist Megaspeed for months as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick feared that the move could worsen trade tensions with China.

articles.title: We tested the RAM-saving storage tech in Gears of War: E-Day
articles.content: Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase. The game brings together several advanced graphics technologies, including Unreal Engine 5’s Nanite and Lumen, MegaLights, and RTX Mega Geometry for more accurate ray-traced shadows and reflections, alongside a range of upscaling and frame generation technologies. However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally important role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage. We’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer. This will allow us to see how much of a difference the technology makes, particularly on lower-end systems. The Storage Tech Explained The Storage Tech Explained In an interview with Digital Foundry, The Coalition explained how they leveraged the Xbox Series S’s fast SSD to bring the dense world of Gears of War: E-Day to a memory-limited system. By effectively using the NVMe SSD as an extension of system memory, they can dynamically load and offload complex city data in real time. This approach allows the game to stream the necessary assets for each scene just in time, overcoming the console’s limited RAM. Digital Foundry notes that the true “special sauce” lies in The Coalition’s smart data management. The team employs advanced heuristics to determine which assets are fetched from the SSD and when, carefully balancing performance. Overusing this technique could harm frame rates, so the system is tuned to swap data only when it benefits the experience. Gears of War: E-Day also supports DirectStorage, although based on our previous testing, this alone does not always result in high SSD activity or read rates. Is this storage tech also used on PC? Is this storage tech also used on PC? YouTuber Mostly Positive Review s shared his findings in a recent post on X, where he found higher-than-usual SSD activity in Task Manager when playing the game. Gears of War E-Day is visually very impressive, but something has to be done with how the game either compiles shaders or streams data.My 14400F is constantly sitting at 80% CPU usage, 16GB RAM is maxed out, and disk read is sitting at a constant 120 MBps, with spikes up to 500 MBps. Will test this with the 9060 XT as well.These are settings I chose to maintain 60 fps, which it does, except for the massive shader compilation stutters every so often. October 7, 2026 Based on his findings, we decided to investigate further. We tested SSD activity across all of the game’s graphics presets at 4K using DLSS Quality. Peak Bandwidth Average Bandwidth Ludicrous 3.7 GB/s 1.3 GB/s Ultra 2.8 GB/s 1.2 GB/s High 2.5 GB/s 1.05 GB/s Medium 1.5 GB/s 824 GB/s Low 858 MB/s 359 GB/s In our previous tests of games that relied heavily on the SSD, none came close to sustaining 1 GB/s of average bandwidth. The highest we recorded was 366 MB/s in Forspoken at 4K with maximum settings, while many titles stayed well under 100 MB/s.…

articles.title: The FAA’s IT troubles are far bigger then AI
articles.content: U.S. airlines are still reeling from a nationwide groundstop issued late Friday night that interrupted weekend travel and wreaked havoc on schedules. The culprit, the Federal Aviation Administration says, was simply outdated tech. The groundstop was followed by eager speculation on social media about what might have caused the issue. Some pointed a finger at a new AI system that the FAA integrated earlier this week; others blamed foreign adversaries. At the same time, a range of tech companies that contract with the FAA (like Microsoft ) were quick to distance themselves from the agency’s problems. Later Friday evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters the outage occurred after an old Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) analog system, an arcane system of processing data signals over a network, became overloaded. This, in turn, impacted the telecommunications systems used by TRACONs, the air traffic control facilities that help direct flights at airports. Duffy noted that systems that had already been upgraded to new internet protocol-based systems did not experience the outage. “This is all the old legacy equipment,” he said Friday . “All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down.” Officials, at least for now, insist there’s no evidence anything nefarious happened. Instead, the Transportation Department is, once again, begging Congress for more money to overhaul FAA tech. Duffy urged Congress to provide additional funding to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system, arguing that the issue should transcend partisan politics. He noted that the FAA had received $15 billion for modernization efforts over the past 25 years, with little to show for it. “It’s not red, it’s not blue, it’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican, it’s American,” he told reporters. “Give us the money to fix it.” Indeed, the FAA’s tech problems are way bigger than AI. Instead, they have a lot more to do with the challenges of updating technology while it’s actively being used. Our pilots guidance system is ancient and isn’t designed to handle upgrades This isn’t the first time the FAA has experienced a major outage that’s brought flights across the country to a halt. Back in 2023, the U.S.’s Notice to Airmen system (NOTAM)—which alerts pilots to potential hazards in American airspace—came offline, after contractors accidentally deleted files that disrupted the program’s core technology. There’s been an ongoing effort to improve the NOTAM system, but it’s moving at a snail’s pace. The FAA has brought in private industry for help and engaged in an effort to modernize the system, but that process has only brought to light myriad other problems. For one, at least according to contract paperwork obtained last year , NOTAMs weren’t exclusively being stored in a virtual environment or in an entirely-digital format. Another aspiration the FAA was working on, at least at the time: making sure that upgrades to some systems didn’t disrupt, well, all of air traffic control. “Everyone will say, ‘well, there’s backups in place,’” Shawn Pruchnicki, a former pilot atOhio State’s Center for Aviation Studies, told FedScoop at the time. “But we’ve also seen time and time again where those things have been said and things have gone horribly wrong.” Poor AI rollout Like a lot of other federal agencies, the Federal Aviation Administration has been inching toward deploying artificial intelligence for a host of applications. Back in 2023, the Transportation Department, which the FAA sits under, even disclosed using ChatGPT for certain purposes (which the FAA, at the time, denied). Since then, though, the FAA begun to embrace AI: A use case inventory released by the government references several use cases, including AI-powered pilot voice transcription, systems for detecting drones, and meteorology. But the FAA hasn’t been the best at communicating how it plans to use AI safely to the public,…
